q: Which is the national animal of India?
e: With its fiery orange coat and mighty prowl, India chose the magnificent tiger to represent the whole nation's strength.

q: Cats have whiskers under their legs.
e: It is true! Sneaky kitties have special whiskers behind their front paws to feel moving critters when they pounce.

q: What animal takes part in Schrödinger's most famous thought experiment?
e: A clever scientist imagined a curious cat hiding inside a closed box to show just how strange tiny particles can be.

q: Kangaroos keep food in their pouches next to their children.
e: That is false! A kangaroo's cozy pouch is strictly a nursery for her baby, not a pocket for storing snacks.

q: What organelle aids in synthesis of DNA in cells?
e: Ribosomes are busy little cell factories that build the proteins needed to help make and copy DNA.

q: What is an example of a bacterial pathogen?
e: Cholera is caused by sneaky bacteria lurking in dirty water that can make a person feel terribly sick.

q: What name is given to all baby marsupials?
e: Whether it grows into a big kangaroo or a sleepy koala, every marsupial baby is warmly called a joey.

q: By definition, where does an abyssopelagic animal live?
a: At the bottom of the ocean
e: These mysterious creatures make their home at the bottom of the ocean, swimming happily in the chilly, pitch-black deep.

q: A slug’s blood is green.
e: This is true! Instead of red, a slug's blood turns a cool green color because it carries oxygen using copper.

q: Which of the following bones is not in the leg?
e: Your radius actually lives in your lower arm, helping your wrist twist around whenever you wave hello.

q: The human heart has how many chambers?
e: Your marvelous heart is split into four little rooms, pumping blood in and out all day long.

q: Snakes and lizards are known to flick their tongue, this behavior is to?
e: That tongue dances into the breeze to capture floating scent bits, helping the snake sniff out its neighborhood.

q: Rhinoplasty is a surgical procedure on what part of the human body?
e: Just like a rhinoceros shows off its mighty snout, a rhinoplasty is a special operation to fix a human nose.

q: Rabbits are carnivores.
e: That is false! Fluffy bunnies are gentle plant-eaters that would much rather munch on sweet grass than eat meat.

q: What did Gregory Mendel use to test genetic crossovers?
e: A curious monk grew thousands of garden peas to see how family traits like height and color pass along.

q: In 2016, the IUCN reclassified the status of Giant Pandas from endangered to vulnerable.
e: It is true! Thanks to protected bamboo forests, growing numbers helped these fluffy giant pandas move safely off the endangered list.

q: Which breed of dog is traditionally associated with firefighters?
e: Energetic, spotted Dalmatians used to run beside horse-drawn wagons, bravely clearing busy streets for firefighters.

q: Elephants are physically unable to jump.
e: It is true! These gentle giants are far too heavy and lack the springy ankles needed to jump into the air.

q: About what percentage of the Earth's surface is water?
e: Looking down from outer space, sparkling blue oceans cover a whopping seventy percent of our watery planet.

q: What is the scientific name for modern day humans?
e: Homo sapiens is our official scientific name, which means wise human in the grand story of life.

q: The biggest distinction between a eukaryotic cell and a prokaryotic cell is:
a: The presence or absence of certain organelles
The presence or absence of a nucleus
e: Eukaryotic cells keep their precious instruction manuals tucked inside a cozy room called a nucleus, while prokaryote cells let theirs float free.

q: The shape of the Earth is a perfect sphere.
e: Our spinning world bulges around its middle like a chubby tummy, making it a slightly squished ball instead of a perfect sphere.

q: A caterpillar has more muscles than humans do.
e: Tiny caterpillars wiggle along using thousands of bendy muscles, while humans only need about six hundred to jump and dance!

q: 71% of the Earth's surface is made up of
e: Looking down from space, our planet wears a giant splash of blue because vast, rolling oceans cover most of its surface.

q: Which is the longest bone in the human body?
e: Tucked inside your thigh, the mighty femur stretches from hip to knee, easily beating every other bone in length.

q: The internet browser Firefox is named after the Red Panda.
e: Even though the browser logo looks like a fiery fox, a firefox is actually another name for the fluffy red panda.

q: What is the fastest  land animal?
e: With paws built like race cars, the speedy cheetah can outrun every other creature sprinting on dry land.

q: What produces the green colour of most plant leaves?
e: Leaves wear bright green coats because they are packed with chlorophyll, a little helper that catches sunshine to make food.

q: Wombats are native to which Country?
e: These chubby, burrow-digging wombats waddle and play naturally across the grassy hills and wild bush of Australia.

q: What is the powerhouse of the cell?
e: Mitochondria act like bustling little power stations, turning the food you eat into energy to keep your cells dancing!

q: What is the thin, outermost layer of the Earth?
e: Just like a fresh loaf of bread, Earth is wrapped in a thin, rocky outer layer called the crust.

q: Rabbits can see what's behind themselves without turning their heads.
e: With wide eyes set high on their heads, bunnies can spot sneaky visitors behind them without even turning around.

q: Rabbits are rodents.
e: Bunnies might nibble like mice, but an extra pair of upper teeth makes them lagomorphs instead of rodents.

q: Hippocampus is the Latin name for which marine creature?
e: This charming sea creature got its Latin name because its curved little head looks just like a tiny horse underwater.

q: The Kākāpō is a large, flightless, nocturnal parrot native to which country?
e: The delightfully pudgy kakapo parrot waddles through the mossy, quiet forests of New Zealand under the starry night sky.

q: Which of these bones is hardest to break?
e: Your sturdy femur is built thick like a tree trunk, making this thigh bone the absolute hardest to break.

q: Human cells typically have how many copies of each gene?
e: You inherit two copies of each gene recipe—one lovingly gifted from your mom, and one from your dad!

q: The Axolotl is an amphibian that can spend its whole life in a larval state.
e: This smiling underwater salamander chooses to never grow up, keeping its feathery baby gills for its entire happy life.

q: How many teeth does an adult rabbit have?
e: Behind those famous bunny grins hide twenty-eight busy teeth, constantly grinding down tough hay and garden greens.

q: A flock of crows is known as a homicide.
e: A big group of these clever black birds is famously called a murder, not a homicide.

q: What colour is the female blackbird?
e: Lady blackbirds wear cozy brown feathers instead of black, helping them hide like little shadows while keeping their eggs safe.

q: Celiac Disease is a disease that effects the heart, causing those effected to be unable to eat meat.
e: This tricky condition actually upsets your tummy whenever you eat gluten found in bread, not meat or your heart.

q: How many legs do butterflies have?
e: Like all proud insects, these fluttery garden dancers have six tiny legs for tiptoeing across sweet flower petals.

q: What is the collective noun for a group of crows?
e: When these clever birds gather together, people call the spooky crew a murder!

q: What is Grumpy Cat's real name?
e: Behind that famous, adorable frown was a sweet little kitty named Tardar Sauce.

q: A bear does NOT defecate during hibernation.
e: During their super-long winter nap, bears shut down their tummies completely and never need a bathroom break.

q: How many bones are in the human body?
e: Inside you right now, 206 sturdy bones work together like a magical team to help you dance!

q: What is the "powerhouse" of the Eukaryotic animal cell?
e: Mitochondria act like tiny, buzzing batteries, happily making all the energy your cells need to keep zooming around.

q: What is the name of a rabbit's abode?
e: Bunnies use their busy paws to dig a burrow, a cozy underground tunnel just right for snuggling.

q: What color is a Steller's Jay?
e: This noisy forest acrobat shows off striking blue feathers below and a midnight-black hood on its clever head.

q: The Killer Whale is considered a type of dolphin.
e: Believe it or not, these giant ocean acrobats are actually the biggest, splashiest dolphins in the sea!

q: Which of these animals are not real?
e: While the others roam our wild world, the Nemean lion lives only in grand old storybooks from ancient Greece.

q: How many chromosomes are in your body cells?
e: Your body cells get 23 pairs of chromosomes, holding the wonderful instruction book that makes you unique.

q: Which class of animals are newts members of?
e: Newts are proud amphibians, starting out swimming with tiny gills before happily exploring damp moss on land.

q: Which of the following blood vessels carries deoxygenated blood?
e: The pulmonary artery rushes tired, oxygen-hungry blood away from your heart straight to your lungs for fresh air!

q: Zebras are white with black stripes.
e: Underneath all that fancy dazzle, zebras actually have black skin and grow white stripes on top.

q: Rabbits can't vomit.
e: Bunnies have super-strong tummy muscles that keep everything locked inside, meaning they never burp or throw up.

q: What is the largest animal currently on Earth?
e: Gliding through deep blue seas, the mighty blue whale is bigger than any creature that has ever lived!

q: What do you call a baby bat?
e: Even though they fly through the night sky, a cozy baby bat is affectionately called a pup.

q: The freshwater amphibian, the Axolotl, can regrow it's limbs.
e: These smiling little water dwellers possess real-life magic, easily regrowing lost legs without even leaving a scar!

q: Which portion of the Marijuana plant produces the psychoactive substance known as THC?
e: The plant makes THC mainly inside its sticky female flowers, using tiny glittering glands to create the powerful chemical.

q: What is the world's longest venomous snake?
e: The king cobra can stretch longer than a whole minivan, reigning as the longest venomous snake on the planet!

q: An octopus can fit through any hole larger than its beak.
e: With no bones inside, an octopus is delightfully squishy and can squeeze through any space bigger than its hard beak.

q: What is the national bird of Bahrain?
e: With its sweet singing voice and friendly charm, the lovely bulbul proudly serves as Bahrain's beloved national bird.

q: What type of animal is a natterjack?
e: Meet the natterjack, a yellow-striped toad that scurries across sandy dunes on little legs instead of hopping!

q: What does "hippopotamus" mean and in what langauge?
e: Long ago, clever Greeks watched this gigantic swimmer splash in the water and named it "river horse."

q: About how much of their body weight in food do sea otters eat every day?
e: To stay warm in chilly ocean waves, a fuzzy sea otter must gobble down a whopping 25 percent of its body weight daily!

q: What are rhino's horn made of?
e: That impressive horn is not bone at all, but tightly packed keratin, the very same stuff that makes your fingernails!

q: "Tachycardia" or "Tachyarrhythmia" refers to a resting heart-rate near or over 100 BPM.
e: It is true, because tachycardia means your resting heart is zipping along at a super-fast speed of one hundred beats each minute!

q: About how old is Earth?
e: Our grand home planet has been spinning around the warm sun for about four and a half billion wondrous years.

q: The Axiom of Preventive Medicine states that people with ___ risk for a disease should be screened and we should treat ___ of those people.
e: This rule focuses on helping everyone in the low risk group, since tiny helps across whole communities prevent the most illness.

q: What is the fastest animal?
e: When this feathered daredevil folds its wings and dives, the peregrine falcon zooms faster than a racecar, beating every creature on Earth.

q: A defibrillator is used to start up a heartbeat once a heart has stopped beating.
e: A defibrillator cannot restart a heart that fully stopped; it actually resets a wildly fluttering heartbeat back to its calm, steady rhythm.

q: What is the name for a male bee that comes from an unfertilized egg?
e: Meet the drone, a gentle boy bee born without a father who spends his sunny days relaxing around the busy hive.

q: The average lifespan of a wildcat is only around 5-6 years.
e: That statement is false because tough wildcats can happily prowl the forests for ten to fifteen long years.

q: Which color cannot be produced in Roses, even through genetic alteration?
e: Roses simply lack the natural blue recipe in their genes, so a true blue petal stays pure fairytale magic.

q: How many baby/milk teeth does a human child have in total?
e: Little kids show off twenty baby teeth before the Tooth Fairy trades them in for grown-up ones!

q: The medial meniscus forms which part of what joint in the human body?
e: Your knee stays happy and bouncy thanks to the medial meniscus, a rubbery little cushion tucked inside.

q: What stage of development do the majority of eukaryotic cells remain in for most of their life?
e: Cells spend most of their cozy lives in interphase, happily growing, eating, and prepping before ever dividing.

q: Anatomy considers the forms of macroscopic structures such as organs and organ systems.
e: It is true that anatomy explores the big, amazing structures you can actually see, like organs and bones!

q: How many teeth does the average adult mouth have (except for wisdom teeth)?
e: A full adult smile lines up thirty-two handy teeth, working like a team of little chompers to crunch your food!

q: The human right lung has how many lobes?
e: With plenty of room on the right side, that lung neatly splits into three breezy lobes to catch your breath.

q: What color/colour is a polar bear's skin?
e: Under all that fluffy white fur, a polar bear actually has black skin to soak up every drop of sunshine!

q: What cell organelle is known as "the powerhouse of the cell?"
e: Mitochondria work like tiny, buzzing power plants, turning your snacks into all the energy you need to zoom around!

q: A carnivorous animal eats flesh, what does a nucivorous animal eat?
e: Just like a busy squirrel packing its cheeks for winter, a nucivorous creature loves crunching on tasty nuts.

q: Cashmere is the wool from which kind of animal?
e: That cloud-soft cashmere sweater actually comes from the warm, fluffy undercoat of mountain goats keeping cozy in chilly winds.

q: Which of the following is NOT a venomous snake?
e: Instead of using venom, the reticulated python is a mighty hugger that wraps around its dinner with pure muscle power.

q: Sea sponges can have hearts.
e: Sea sponges live a very relaxed life without any hearts at all, happily letting ocean currents do all the pumping for them.

q: How many hearts does an octopus have?
e: An octopus has three big hearts beating together, working as a team to pump blue blood through its chilly ocean home.

q: Which of these species is not extinct?
e: While the others have vanished into history, mighty Komodo dragons are still happily stomping around their sunny island homes today!

q: What is the colour of unoxidized blood?
e: Even when it is resting and low on fresh oxygen, your blood is always a cozy, deep red shade.

q: The dish Fugu, is made from what family of fish?
e: Chefs prepare fugu from the spiky pufferfish, carefully slicing away danger so brave diners can taste this famous round swimmer!

q: The now extinct species "Thylacine" was native to where?
e: The striped thylacine, also known as the Tasmanian tiger, once roamed wild across the grassy hills of Tasmania, Australia.

q: What is the Linnean name of the domestic apple tree?
e: Scientists gave the sweet domestic apple tree the fancy, ancient name Malus pumila to officially identify this crunchy orchard favorite.

q: The "mountain chicken" is a chicken.
e: Nature loves surprises; the mountain chicken isn't a feathered bird at all, but a giant, croaking frog!

q: What dog breed is one of the oldest breeds of dog and has flourished since before 400 BCE.
e: With their cute wrinkled faces, charming pugs were already beloved royal lapdogs over two thousand years ago!

q: The Platypus is a mammal.
e: Even though this quirky duck-billed swimmer lays eggs, it feeds its babies milk, making it a true mammal!

q: Which of these is NOT a bone found in the human arm?
e: Your arm bones love waving hello, but the sturdy tibia lives way down in your lower leg!

q: "Decapods" are an order of ten-footed crustaceans.  Which of these are NOT decapods?
e: While lobsters strut on ten legs, tiny krill paddle through the sea with feathery swimming feet, so they aren't decapods!

q: Which of the following is true when alligators are behaving territorially?
a: They run full force at the threat
Slap their tails on the ground
Open their jaws while making a clicking noise
They bellow while showing their tail and neck
e: To say this swamp is mine, a grumpy alligator arches its neck, lifts its tail, and roars a deep bellow.

q: Which animal was part of an Russian domestication experiment in 1959?
e: Russian scientists gently picked the friendliest wild foxes, discovering that sweet pups soon grew floppy ears and wagging tails!

q: What part of the brain takes its name from the Greek for seahorse?
e: Tucked inside your brain, the memory-making hippocampus curls up looking just like a tiny seahorse, which is what its name means!

q: The Ceratosaurus, a dinosaur known for having a horn on the top of its nose, is also known to be a decendent of the Tyrannosaurus Rex.
e: That is false! Ceratosaurus actually stomped around millions of years before T. rex ever arrived on the scene.

q: Tigers have one colour of skin despite the stripey fur.
e: That is false! A tiger's famous stripes are actually printed right on its skin, hidden underneath that fuzzy coat.

q: What is the common term for bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE)?
e: This brain sickness makes cattle wobble and act strangely, earning it the famous everyday nickname Mad Cow disease.

q: In human biology, a circadium rhythm relates to a period of roughly how many hours?
e: Tucked inside you is a cozy little clock that runs for roughly 24 hours, deciding when you wake up and when you yawn.

q: What are the smallest blood vessels in the human body?
e: Capillaries are so wonderfully tiny that red blood cells must march through them in a single-file line!

q: What is the medical term for low blood sugar?
e: Hypoglycemia happens when your body's fuel tank runs low on sugar, leaving your energy engines feeling sleepy.

q: When was the first mammal successfully cloned?
e: Back in 1996, scientists made history by welcoming Dolly the sheep, the very first cloned mammal!

q: What do you study if you are studying entomology?
e: Entomology is all about exploring the buzzing, crawling, six-legged world of insects!

q: What is the scientific name for the "Polar Bear"?
e: Scientists call the polar bear Ursus maritimus, meaning sea bear, because this snowy giant loves paddling through icy waters.

q: Otters have pockets under their arms for carrying their favourite snacks and rocks.
e: Believe it or not, otters really do have loose skin folds under their arms that act as pockets for their favorite pebbles!

q: What is the collective noun for rats?
e: When a clever bunch of scampering rats huddle together, this playful squad is delightfully called a mischief!

q: What is the name of the family that the domestic cat is a member of?
e: Every purring pet cat belongs to Felidae, the grand family tree that also includes mighty lions and speedy cheetahs!

q: Down Syndrome is usually caused by an extra copy of which chromosome?
e: Down syndrome happens when cells accidentally pack an extra third copy of little chromosome 21 into the suitcase of life.

q: What is the collective noun for bears?
e: A cozy group of sleepy bears lumbering together through the woods is delightfully called a sloth.

q: What causes Lyme disease?
e: Sneaky corkscrew-shaped bacteria hitch a ride on tiny ticks, sneaking inside their host to cause Lyme disease.

q: Male pandas do handstands while urinating on trees.
e: It is true! Male pandas do acrobatic handstands on tree trunks so their smelly scent marks reach high into the breeze.

q: Hyenas are more closely related to cats than to dogs.
e: Believe it or not, it is true! Beneath that dog-like laugh, hyenas actually belong on the cat branch of nature's family tree.

q: What is the study of the cells and tissues of plants and animals?
e: Histology is the wonderful science of peering through a microscope to explore the cozy neighborhoods of plant and animal tissues.

q: The "Gympie Stinger" is the deadliest plant in the world.
e: That prickly bush packs a fiercely painful sting, but other sneaky plants hold much deadlier poisons.

q: "Kamea," the Gilbertese Islander word for dog, is derived from the English phrase "Come here!"
e: Pups eagerly ran whenever sailors shouted 'Come here,' so islanders turned that friendly call into their word for dog.

q: You can tell the age of a ladybird by counting the spots on his back.
e: Those cute polka dots reveal what kind of beetle it is, not how many birthdays it has celebrated.

q: Approximately how long is a year on Uranus?
e: That chilly blue giant takes a whopping 84 Earth years just to complete one slow orbit around the sun.

q: The medical condition osteoporosis affects which part of the body?
e: This condition quietly sneaks inside your bones, turning a sturdy skeleton brittle and weak.

q: What are the scales on all snakes and most lizards are made of?
e: A snake wears a shiny suit of keratin, the exact same tough stuff found in your own fingernails.

q: What is the average lifespan of a domestic rabbit?
e: With plenty of crunchy greens and love, pet bunnies happily thump along for eight to twelve years.

q: The echidna is a monotreme.
e: This spiky little marvel belongs to the monotreme family because it lays eggs instead of giving live birth.

q: Which dog breed is named after a region in Croatia
e: These playful, spotty dogs get their name from Dalmatia, a sunny coastal region tucked away in Croatia.

q: Pneumonoultramicroscopicsilicovolcanoconiosis is a synonym for the disease known as silicosis.
e: That monster of a word is just a fancy name for silicosis, caused by breathing fine volcanic dust.

q: The most frequent subconscious activity repeated by the human body is blinking.
e: While your eyelids flutter a lot, your steady heartbeat and quiet breaths happen far more often each day.

q: What is the scientific name of the Common Chimpanzee?
e: Pan troglodytes is the special scientific name given to our clever, fruit-loving chimpanzee cousins.

q: For what reason would a spotted hyena "laugh"?
e: That spooky chuckle is not a happy giggle; hyenas actually laugh when they feel nervous and stressed.

q: Myopia is the scientific term for which condition?
e: Myopia is shortsightedness, making distant trees look blurry while a cozy book up close stays crystal clear.

q: Which of the following is the male pollen-producing reproductive part of a flower?
e: Like tiny dusted wands, stamens stand tall inside the flower to make golden pollen for visiting bees.

q: Which part of the body does glaucoma affect?
e: Glaucoma builds up sneaking pressure inside the eyes, threatening the wondrous windows you see the world with.

q: Finnish Lapphund dogs were used for herding reindeer.
e: Wearing warm fuzzy coats, these brave pups spent centuries helping people round up and guide reindeer herds.

q: Microscopic zooplankton [ZOH-oh-plank-ton] can best be classified as which of the following trophic levels?
e: These tiny ocean wanderers are herbivores, happily grazing on microscopic green plants drifting in the sea.

q: Which of the following has been most greatly and directly altered by human activity in the biosphere?
e: By burning fuels and farming, humans have drastically stirred up Earth's natural chemical cycles of carbon and nitrogen.

q: A newborn baby was found to have 47 chromosomes. What is the term for this disorder?
e: When a baby ends up with an extra chromosome instead of forty-six, scientists call this uneven count aneuploidy.

q: Immunoglobulins are an example of which of the following?
e: These microscopic defenders, also called antibodies, are specially folded proteins built like tiny grabber tools to catch sneaky germs.

q: Which of the following is an example of a change in the primary structure of a protein?
a: A protein folding into a beta sheet
e: A protein is like a beaded necklace, so swapping just one amino acid bead changes its original chain pattern.

q: Which of the following human diseases is dominant?
e: Huntington's disease is dominant because just a single copy of that bossy gene is enough to cause the illness.

q: Human infants weighing more or less than the average birth weight of 6 to 8 pounds have a greater chance of mortality. Which of the following types of natural selection describes this phenomenon?
e: Stabilizing selection favors the cozy middle, helping average-weight babies thrive by steering clear of risky extremes.

q: Which of the following neurotransmitters is utilized at all vertebrate neuromuscular junctions?
e: Whenever your brain tells a muscle to move, acetylcholine is the busy chemical messenger that rushes over to trigger the twitch.

q: Introducing rabbits in Australia that eat the same food and use the same space for burrows as native marsupials is what type of species interaction?
e: When newcomers and locals tussle over the same cozy burrows and leafy snacks, that neighborhood rivalry is called competition.

q: Which of the following accurately matches the part of the flower and its description?
a: Top part of the stamen that produces and bears pollen - sepal
Swollen base of the flower than attaches it to the stem - carpel
Sticky part of the flower's carpel that traps pollen grains - stigma
Part of the flower containing the ovules that later develop into seeds - anther
e: Like a sweet little landing pad, the stigma stays super sticky so it can trap passing grains of pollen!

q: Exopolymeric substances, or EPS, are exuded by microorganisms during times of environmental stress. Which of the following is NOT a function of EPS?
e: This gooey slime shields germs from drying out, but it cannot feed them, so it offers no protection against starvation.

q: Which of the following is a distinguishing characteristic of cheetah paws?
a: Their claws are covered with a sheath of skin
e: Cheetahs cannot fully pull their claws back, using them like built-in cleats to grip the ground during speedy chases!

q: Which of the following is a disadvantage of inbreeding?
a: Farmers get to choose what organisms to breed
The inbred organism may have genetic disorders due to similar alleles
Unlike hybrids, inbred organisms are not very valuable to people
e: When close relatives have babies, matching hidden hiccups in their genes can easily double up and cause harmful disorders.

q: Which of the following plant cell components is responsible for making a connection between the cytoplasm of adjacent cells?
e: Plasmodesmata are like tiny secret doorways between plant cells, letting friendly neighbors share messages and sips of water.

q: Glucose, sucrose, fructose, and lactose are all examples of which of the following?
e: These sweet names are all carbohydrates, sugary little fuel packs that give your body quick energy to run and play!

q: Which of the following cell types would be most important for an allergy response?
e: Basophils sound the alarm during allergies, releasing chemicals that make your nose tickle and sneeze!

q: Amylase [AM-il-ace] catalyzes the digestion of starch into sugars. The presence of high amounts of amylase in the blood is likely to be associated with dysfunction of which of the following organs?
e: Your pancreas is the hard-working chef that cooks up amylase, so too much in your blood means it needs help.

q: Which of the following parts of the brain is responsible for controlling heart rate and breathing?
e: Tucked low in your brain, the trusty medulla works quietly behind the scenes to keep your heart beating and lungs breathing.

q: In bean and corn seeds, the food supply that is used by the seed to germinate and grow is found in the:
e: Think of the cotyledon as a cozy lunchbox, feeding the tiny baby sprout until it can taste sunshine!

q: Which of the following is most accurate about the pasteurization of milk:
a: it kills all bacteria by sterilizing the milk
it reduces the population of bacteria by heating but not boiling the milk
e: Pasteurization gently warms milk just enough to defeat harmful bacteria without boiling away all the creamy goodness.

q: Hirudinea [HEER-oo-din-ee-ah] is a class that contains which of the following organisms?
e: Leeches belong to the Hirudinea family, squirming through the water like little stretchy ribbons looking for a warm snack.

q: Which of the following correctly explains why glucose is converted to glucose-6-phosphate in the first step of glycolysis [glye-KAWL-eh-sis]?
a: The cell membrane is impermeable to large, negatively-charged molecules
It enables the splitting of glucose in half during the next step
The isomerization [eye-saw-mor-eyes-AY-shun] of glucose is less favorable than that of glucose-6-phosphate
Glucose-6-phosphate can also be incorporated into glycogen [GLYE-koh-jen]
e: Adding a charged tag traps glucose inside, because the cell membrane will not let large, negative molecules slip away.

q: Which of the following is the most likely highest power for an objective lens on a typical student compound light microscope:
e: A 100-times lens is the strongest regular glass eye on a student microscope, zooming into tiny worlds without crashing slides.

q: Ubiquitin [you-BIH-kwih-tin] tags can be used to direct proteins to a proteasome [PRO-tee-uh-zohm]. What happens to the protein there?
a: It is sent to the nucleus
e: The proteasome acts like a hungry recycling machine, eagerly chomping tagged old proteins into tiny reusable scraps.

q: Which of the following is the BEST explanation for what would happen to a red blood cell if it were placed in a 25% sugar solution:
a: it would lose salt to the sugar solution and gain sugar and remain the same size
it would gain salt and swell
it would lose water to the sugar solution and gain salt and remain the same size
it would lose water to the sugar solution and shrink
e: Surrounded by thick, thirsty sugar water, the red blood cell loses its own water and wrinkles up like a tiny raisin.

q: Which of the following is the BEST explanation why fruit flies are popular experimental organisms in genetic studies:
a: they are true breeding with almost no mutations and have only two chromosomes
they are cheap to maintain, produce many offspring, and have a short time between generations
they are very safe, carry no human diseases, and have only two chromosomes
their genes are extra-sensitive to mutation-causing substances, which makes them excellent to observe evolving under stress
e: Fruit flies are tiny science champions because they grow up fast, cost pennies, and quickly welcome hundreds of babies.

q: Before a protein can be made, a gene must first be transcribed into what molecule?
e: A gene passes its secret recipe to messenger RNA, sending this tiny courier off to build brand-new proteins.

q: Eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells both contain:
e: Every single cell, tiny or grand, wraps itself in a soft cell membrane to keep its precious insides safe.

q: If an animal has 42 chromosomes in its normal, non-gamete or somatic cells, what term would be given to the gametes that have 21 chromosomes:
e: Carrying just half the usual recipe of chromosomes, these special little cells are known as haploid.

q: Which of the following is an example of a protist?
e: Kelp might look like an underwater tree, but this leafy organism is actually a massive protist dancing in the sea.

q: Which of the following statements does NOT support the cell theory?
a: All organisms are composed of cells
Cells are the fundamental units of living organisms
e: Cells cannot just poof out of thin air! Every tiny cell alive today came from another cell that lived before it.

q: Which of the following functional groups is possessed by alcohols?
e: Every alcohol molecule proudly wears a hydroxyl group, where an oxygen and a hydrogen atom hold hands like best friends.

q: On an island, half of one species of birds has small beaks and the other half has large beaks. A tree with small seeds is very prevalent on the island; hundreds of years later, the small-beaked birds outnumber the large-beaked birds. According to the principles of natural selection, which of the following is the most likely explanation?
a: Birds with small beaks were better able to fight birds with large beaks
Large beaks gradually shrunk due to the smaller available food
Birds with small beaks were most likely to forage successfully, and were thus more likely to reproduce
Birds with large beaks are likely to have more offspring
e: Birds with small beaks gathered food easily, stayed healthy, and had lots of chicks that inherited those handy little beaks.

q: Which of the following cellular components is present in eukaryotes [YOO-care-ee-oats], but not prokaryotes [PRO-care-ee-oats]?
e: Eukaryote cells keep their precious DNA tucked safely inside a cozy little headquarters called a nucleus, while simpler prokaryotes let theirs float freely.

q: What is the endocrine gland that controls how the body regulates metabolism and is associated with Graves' disease?
e: Perched in your neck like a butterfly, the thyroid gland sets your body's energy speed and gets overexcited in Graves' disease.

q: When you are sick with a virus, your body builds up a defense system by making antibodies against it. Why, then, do we need to get flu shots every year?
a: Antibodies are usually only effective for a few months
We need antibiotics to combat the flu
We could be flu carriers even if we are not sick
The flu virus mutates every year
e: Sneaky flu viruses love wearing new disguises, mutating each year so your body needs a fresh wanted poster to spot them!

q: In which of the following areas of the human body is the ileum bone found:
e: Your pelvis features the wide, curving ilium bone, proudly helping your hips hold up the rest of your body.

q: To which of the following virus classes does HIV belong?
e: HIV is a retrovirus because it works backward, turning its genetic recipe upside down to sneak into healthy cells.

q: Which of the following statements is NOT true about slime mold?
a: It lacks chitin in its cell walls
e: Even with mold in its name, slime mold is actually a clever protist that wanders around eating, not a real fungus!

q: Which of the following types of trees includes individuals that were saplings when the great pyramids were built and are still alive today?
e: High on windy mountaintops, ancient bristlecone pines have quietly stood watch for thousands of years, living long before the pyramids were finished!

q: If a cell is placed in a hypotonic solution, what effect will osmosis have on the cell?
a: It will become turgid or lyse
e: Water rushes inside like a filling balloon, making the plant cell puff up tight or even burst open!

q: What is the limiting factor for phytoplankton productivity in the tropical open ocean?
e: Even under warm sunny skies, floating plankton cannot grow big and strong without tasty mineral nutrients to feed on.

q: What characteristic is most likely to identify two organisms as the same species?
a: All of their physical characteristics are very similar
They fill the same role in the ecosystem
They are of similar size and shape
e: When two creatures have babies that can grow up and have babies of their own, that proves they belong to the same species.

q: The presence of which of the following is what makes rough endoplasmic reticulum appear rough and not smooth?
e: Tiny protein-making dots called ribosomes speckle the surface like bumpy sprinkles, making this cellular helper look totally rough.

q: Which of the following is the largest songbird in North America?
e: With glossy black feathers and a huge wingspan, the clever common raven towers over every other songbird in North America.

q: Which of the following properties of water allow tall trees to transport water to the canopy?
e: Water molecules hold hands tightly and cling to tree walls, helping them climb all the way to the tippity-top leaves!

q: Which of the following genetic mutations would cause the greatest change in the nucleotide sequence of a gene?
e: Slipping in just one extra base shifts the entire reading frame, scrambling every single three-letter genetic word that comes after!

q: Which of the following is an ectoparasite:
e: Sneaky lice are ectoparasites because they live on the outside of your body, clinging right to hair!

q: When present in large numbers, which of the following can cause red tides?
e: When billions of tiny dinoflagellates gather together for an ocean party, their reddish bodies paint the water into a red tide!

q: Which of the following does NOT occur during prometaphase [pro- MEHTA-phase]?
a: Chromatids [CROW-mah-tids] arrive at opposite cell poles
Kinetochores [kin-EHT-oh-cores] form as proteins attached to centromeres [SEN-troh-meers]
e: The twin chromatids are still getting ready to dance, saving their big trip to opposite poles for much later in the show!

q: Which of the following traits would you expect an ornithopod [AWR-nuh-thuh-pod] dinosaur to have?
e: The word ornithopod secretly means 'bird foot,' so these prehistoric giants stomped around on bird-like toes!

q: In which of the following stages in the life of an average dividing cell would it spend most of its time:
e: Cells spend most of their busy days in interphase, growing big and copying recipes before splitting into two!

q: Which of the following is most advantageous to plants that depend on insects for pollination:
e: Sticky pollen acts like tiny patches of Velcro, happily hitching a ride on fuzzy bee legs to visit neighboring flowers.

q: Which of the following birds depends almost entirely on man-made nesting boxes in the eastern United States?
e: Purple martins love human neighbors so much that in the east, they raise their chicks almost entirely inside cozy birdhouses we build for them!

q: Keratin and hemoglobin are both examples of which of the following macromolecules?
e: Whether giving your hair strength or zooming oxygen through your blood, keratin and hemoglobin are both hardworking proteins.

q: Some inhibitors, rather than competing with the substrate at the active site, bind to a distal site on the enzyme to inhibit activity. What type of inhibition is this?
e: In allosteric inhibition, a sneaky blocker taps a special side spot, gently changing the enzyme's shape so work quietly stops.

q: Which of the following structures in the chicken egg is analogous to the mammalian placenta?
e: Just like a placenta helps human babies, the allantois acts as a caring chick's nursery sack for breathing and holding waste.

q: A geneticist breeds two pea plants that are heterozygous for seed color. Given that 2001 of the F2 generation are homozygous recessive, which of the following is closest to the number of plants that exhibit the dominant trait?
e: For every quiet plant showing the hidden trait, three proud plants show the dominant one, giving us about 6,006 colorful sprouts!

q: The kingdom Plantae [PLAN-tee] consists of members that are which of the following?
e: Plants are bustling neighborhoods of complex eukaryotic cells, teaming up to catch golden sunshine and make their own delicious food.

q: Which of the following statements is true regarding thymine [THIGH-meen], cytosine [sigh-toh-seen], and uracil [YUR-ah-sil]?
a: They can all be found in RNA
They can all be found in DNA
e: Cytosine, thymine, and uracil are all pyrimidines, sharing a neat, single-ring shape to help spell out genetic messages.

q: Which of the following is closest to the length of time it takes for a typical human cell to complete mitosis:
e: Making a brand-new copy is a big job, taking a busy human cell about one whole day to divide!

q: Within the land plants, which of the following groups has the greatest number of species?
e: With hundreds of thousands of colorful cousins blooming everywhere, flowering plants easily outnumber all other plant families on land.

q: Which of the following is an example of a carbohydrate?
e: Glucose is a sweet simple sugar, making it the classic carbohydrate fuel that powers everything from playground tag to daydreaming.

q: What is the largest terrestrial biome, characterized by large populations of coniferous [koh-NIH-fur-us] trees?
e: The chilly taiga stretches across the north like a giant green blanket, packed with millions of pointy cone-bearing trees.

q: A pair of gene homologs are from a mouse and a human, respectively. Which of the following gene regions is likely to be most well-conserved?
e: Exons hold the precious recipes for building working proteins, so nature keeps them carefully protected across humans and mice.

q: Which of the following is true of osmosis?
a: Osmosis is the movement of water from a region of high solute concentration to a region of low solute concentration
Osmosis is a form of passive transport
Osmosis cannot occur across a semi-permeable membrane
Osmosis involves the active transport of solute and requires ATP
e: Osmosis is passive transport because water flows across barriers all on its own, without the cell spending any energy.

q: Which of the following is a rasp-like feeding structure found in many mollusks:
e: Snails and other mollusks scrape up their dinner using a radula, a wondrous tongue covered in tiny, file-like teeth.

q: Which of the following is NOT a member of the order Cetacea?
e: Gentle, slow-swimming manatees are sirenians related to elephants, not cetaceans like speedy dolphins and whales.

q: Often, an enzyme requires the presence of another small molecule in order to function. What is the term for these small molecules?
e: Enzymes are superstar workers, but they need trusty sidekick molecules called cofactors to help them do their jobs!

q: Which of the following is a lipid:
e: Lipids are just slippery fats and oils, so golden corn oil fits right into this greasy little family.

q: Which of the following is the primary reason for a cell to undergo arrest at the G2-M checkpoint of the cell cycle?
a: Chromosomes not attached to spindle fibers
e: A careful cell slams on the brakes if its precious DNA instruction book is missing pages and not fully copied yet.

q: Which of the following would be considered an autotroph (read as: AW-toh-tref)?
e: An oak tree is an autotroph because it catches sunshine with green leaves to bake its own food from scratch!

q: Plants are important to our ecosystem because they convert solar energy into which of the following forms of energy?
e: Green leaves catch warm sunbeams and magically bake that light into sweet chemical energy to feed the world.

q: Which of the following is NOT part of the human respiratory system?
e: Your esophagus is a busy food slide heading straight to your tummy, so it belongs to digestion, not breathing.

q: Which of the following North American spiders' bite could be fatal to humans?
e: Shy as it looks, the brown recluse packs venom so potent that its rare bite can actually be dangerous to humans.

q: The reactions that the cell uses to harvest energy from sugars can be classified as what?
e: Cells harvest sweet energy by passing electrons back and forth like a hot potato during redox reactions.

q: Which of the following is the pH of the normal human stomach lumen?
e: Your stomach is a bubbly little cauldron with strong digestive acid at a pH of 2 to 3 to melt down lunch.

q: What is the name of the respiratory disease that is categorized by the inflammation of the mucus membrane?
e: When your breathing tubes get irritated and swollen with sticky mucus, doctors call that grumpy chest tickle bronchitis.

q: Which of the following is NOT considered connective tissue?
e: Connective tissues act like glue holding parts together, but muscles do their own bouncy work of squeezing and pulling!

q: A series of amino acids joined together will make a:
e: When amino acids click together in a long chain, they fold into a hardworking protein ready to help your body.

q: Most scientists believe that protists evolved from which of the following?
e: Long ago, simpler prokaryote cells took a giant leap forward, growing bigger and more organized to become the very first protists.

q: Which of the following does not demonstrate external radial symmetry?
e: Round sea anemones spread out like bicycle wheels, but wiggly eels have matching left and right sides instead.

q: Of the following habitats, which is the most likely to have the highest amount of biodiversity?
e: Warm, rainy tropical rainforests are bursting with more colorful critters and buzzing life than anywhere else on Earth!

q: Photosynthesis has both light and dark reactions. Which of the following occurs without the presence of light?
a: Water is split to produce oxygen
Carbon dioxide is transformed to sugar
e: Even when the sun goes to sleep, busy plants quietly knit carbon dioxide into sweet, energizing sugar.

q: Which of the following is NOT an autoimmune disease?
e: Unlike autoimmune mix-ups where your body fights itself, shingles is actually caused by a sneaky chickenpox virus waking up.

q: Which of the following statements about wood in a tree is NOT true?
a: Wood is made of secondary xylem [ZY-luhm] and fibers
The oldest wood is at the center of the tree while younger wood is towards the periphery
Annual rings consist of both early (spring) wood and late (summer) wood
True wood is only found in monocots, while dicots do not produce true wood
e: Monocots like grasses and palms cannot make true wood; that sturdy trick belongs to dicots like oak trees and conifers.

q: Which of the following organisms cannot perform photosynthesis?
e: Mushrooms might sprout in the soil, but they lack green chlorophyll and must absorb decaying snacks instead of cooking with sunshine.

q: Which of the following determines the sex of a turtle egg?
e: Warm, cozy sand tucks the turtle eggs in and tells nature whether to hatch baby girls or baby boys.

q: Which of the following types of molecules is not generally composed of a long chain of monomers?
e: Unlike giant chains of repeating building blocks, a fatty acid is just a single tidy molecule standing on its own.

q: What is the protein that binds nuclear material in DNA?
e: Histones act like tidy little spools, letting long threads of DNA wrap snugly around them to fit inside the nucleus.

q: Which of the following statements about human intestinal fluid is NOT true?
a: It is a clear, yellow fluid
Five or six liters of intestinal fluid are produced each day
It has a slightly basic pH of 7.6
e: Your tummy makes only one or two liters of digestive juice each day, not five or six, which would simply be too much!

q: Which of the following is NOT an accurate comparison between meiosis [my-OH-sis] and mitosis [my-TOH-sis]?
a: During metaphase in mitosis, chromosomes line up at the equator, while during metaphase I, homologous [huh-MOL-uh-guhs] pairs line up at the equator
In prophase in mitosis, chromosomes are made of two sister chromatids [KROH-muh-tids], while in prophase I, homologous chromosomes form tetrads
In both anaphase in mitosis and anaphase I of meiosis, sister chromatids separate
Mitosis produces two identical cells, while meiosis produces four daughter cells
e: During anaphase one, sister chromatids hold hands and stay together while pairs split, so they do not separate in both!

q: The green pigment in plants that captures the energy of sunlight and initiates photosynthesis is called:
e: Chlorophyll is the plant's green solar panel, soaking up bright sunshine to help turn light into food.

q: Which of the following anatomical structures do sharks NOT possess:
e: Unlike other fish wearing bony little gill covers, sharks let their open gill slits flap freely in the rushing sea.

q: Which of the following is the location of the biceps humoris muscle:
e: When you proudly flex to show your strength, that big muscle popping up in your arm is your biceps.

q: When basophils react to a foreign substance, they secrete a signaling molecule that causes blood vessels to dilate and leak fluid at the site of inflammation. What is this signaling molecule?
e: When trouble arrives, basophils sound the alarm by releasing histamine, opening blood vessels wide to rush in healing helpers!

q: Cell theory, one of the most fundamental principles of modern biology, consists of three main ideas. Which of the following is NOT one of cell theory's main ideas?
a: All organisms are composed of one or more cells
The cell is the basic unit of organization for organisms
All cells come from preexisting cells
e: Cell theory is all about how living things are built, so causing infectious disease was never invited to join its big rules.

q: Which of the following best describes why humans are unable to digest cellulose?
e: Our stomachs simply lack the special chemical scissors, called enzymes, needed to chop tough plant cellulose into tiny bites.

q: Which of the following amino acids is NOT made by the human body?
e: Our bodies cannot build phenylalanine from scratch, so we must happily welcome this essential building block through the foods we eat.

q: If you put a bacterium with a plasmid for antibiotic resistance into a growth medium with antibiotic, virtually all of the population grown from the starting bacterium will have a copy of the plasmid. However, if you take the same starting bacterium and put it in a growth medium without an antibiotic, many of the progeny will NOT have a copy of the plasmid. Which of the following is the BEST explanation for this observation?
a: Plasmids can be transferred from one bacterium to another
Plasmids have to be beneficial to be replicated
Plasmids are permanent in a population
e: Carrying extra DNA costs energy, so bacteria only keep their helpful plasmids when they truly need them to survive.

q: Which of the following organisms has a hydrostatic skeleton?
e: Without hard bones inside, a sea star relies on water pressure trapped within its body to hold its shape and crawl.

q: Which of the following is an intracellular parasite:
e: The sneaky malaria parasite loves to hide right inside red blood cells, making itself a cozy intracellular home.

q: Ornamentation often contributes to the mating behavior and choices of animals. Male elks are highly ornamented. Which of the following types of mating system would you expect?
e: Bull elk show off giant antlers to win a whole herd of female admirers, a grand family style called polygyny!

q: What organ in the human body is responsible for storing glucose in the form of glycogen [GLY-kuh-juhn]?
e: Your liver works like a faithful pantry, packing extra sugar away as glycogen until you need a burst of energy.

q: What organ in the human body is responsible for storing glucose in the form of glycogen?
e: Think of your liver as a cozy pantry, neatly packing away sugary snacks as glycogen until your body needs a boost!

q: What is the term for the site on an enzyme that a substrate binds to?
e: An enzyme's active site is like a special VIP parking spot, perfectly shaped for just one helper molecule to click right in.

q: Which of the following processes does not add carbon dioxide to the atmosphere?
e: While other processes puff carbon dioxide out, hungry green leaves breathe it in during photosynthesis to make food.

q: A plasmid is a circular DNA molecule that is separate from chromosomal DNA, usually occurring in bacteria. Which of the following do plasmids usually contain?
e: Plasmids are tiny circles of DNA that travel light, usually holding just one or two handy bonus genes for a bacterium.

q: Which of the following BEST describes muscle tone:
a: length versus width of a muscle
average energy use or oxygen use of a fully contracted muscle
amount of tension or contraction of a resting muscle
e: Even when you are snoozing, your muscles keep a tiny bit of tension called muscle tone so they are always ready to spring into action.

q: During the Deep Water Horizon oil spill, marine microbes were observed to consume some of the released hydrocarbons. Which of the following crude oil components is most likely to be degraded quickly by marine microbes?
e: Ethane is tiny and simple, making it a quick, bite-sized snack that hungry microbes can gobble up in a snap.

q: Which of the following organisms exhibits radial symmetry?
e: Shaped like a living wheel, a sea star's matching arms spread outward in a circle from its center.

q: Plasmodium falciparum [plaz-MOH-dee-uhm fal-see-PUH- room] is one of four causative agents of malaria in humans and, like the other three, is which of the following?
e: This sneaky malaria germ is a protozoan, a tiny one-celled critter that hitches a ride inside mosquitoes to cause trouble.

q: Which of the following terms describes the ability of a mutation in gene X to affect the expression of gene Y?
e: With epistasis, one gene acts like a sneaky boss, stepping in to control how another gene shows up.

q: You go to the doctor because you have a sore throat. She looks at your throat and sympathizes, then says, "Go home and rest, you'll beat that virus in no time!" She does NOT write a prescription for antibiotics, however, because:
a: Antibiotics kill bacteria and you have a viral infection
Antibiotics only work if you have a cold
e: Antibiotics only target pesky bacteria, so they are completely powerless against the sneaky little viruses causing your sniffles.

q: Which of the following is NOT true about the human eye:
a: the cornea acts as a lens with a fixed shape
images that are formed on the retina are inverted
most of the eye is filled with a liquid called the aqueous humor
vitamin A is important for light absorbing molecules critical in vision
e: Most of our eyeball is actually packed with squishy vitreous jelly, not the watery aqueous liquid up front.

q: Which of the following types of microscopes passes negatively charged particles guided by magnetic lenses through a very thin specimen, all in a partial vacuum, to produce an image at high magnification:
e: A transmission electron microscope shoots tiny beams straight through super thin slices, revealing secret worlds hidden deep inside cells!

q: A bacterium is suddenly immersed in a high salt media. What is the MOST likely response of the cell?
a: Actively transport water into the cell
Actively transport water out of the cell
Actively transport potassium into the cell
Actively transport small organic molecules out of the cell
e: Surrounded by salty water, the tiny bacterium rushes potassium inside itself to keep its own moisture from escaping.

q: Which of the following compounds is found in the greatest abundance in animals?
e: Animals are basically wonderful, walking puddles, because everyday water makes up most of their bodies!

q: Which of the following is NOT a distinguishing characteristic of members of the subphylum Crustacea?
a: Walking legs present on the abdomen
e: Crustaceans wear their walking legs along their chest, so having walking legs on the abdomen is definitely not a crustacean trait.

q: What organism acts as the vector of malaria in humans?
e: The Anopheles mosquito accidentally carries the malaria parasite from person to person when it stops by for a sip.

q: Which of the following animals would you have to eat in order to ingest a potentially lethal dose of tetrodotoxin [te-troh-duh-TOK-sin]?
e: Round little puffer fish carry dangerous tetrodotoxin inside their bellies to keep hungry sea critters from taking a bite!

q: A small human lymphocyte and a red blood cell are both about how many micrometers across:
e: At eight tiny micrometers wide, these hardworking cells are just the right size to squeeze through your skinniest blood vessels.

q: Which of the following sets of two light colors do chloroplast pigments absorb most effectively during photosynthesis?
e: Plants reflect green light away, but they hungrily drink up red and blue light to power their food factories.

q: A diver finds an underwater cave filled with bacteria that seem to feed on volcanic sulfur vents. What type of organisms are these?
e: Far from sunlight, these chemotrophs power themselves by feasting on hot volcanic chemicals bubbling up from the earth.

q: Which of the following is NOT an effect of the sympathetic nervous system?
e: In fight-or-flight mode, your body widens your eyes to spot danger, so constriction of pupils is not part of the rush.

q: Which of the following neurotransmitters is NOT generally inhibitory?
e: While other brain messengers whisper for quiet, peppy glutamate excites nerve cells and tells them to fire away!

q: Which of the following biomes, on average, receives the lowest amount of annual precipitation?
e: Even though it looks chilly, the tundra is actually a frozen desert that gets less rain and snow than almost anywhere else!

q: Where are DNA molecules located in prokaryotes?
e: Without a nucleus to tuck it into bed, a bacterium lets its DNA float freely in the soupy cytoplasm.

q: During the summer months, which of the following plant structures is NOT a sugar sink?
e: In warm summer sunshine, busy leaves are bustling factories making sweet sugar for everyone else, not storing it for themselves.

q: If a population initially exhibits logistic growth, which of the following bests describes the net population growth rate after the population reaches the carrying capacity?
e: When an animal neighborhood runs completely out of room, new births and deaths balance out, making the growth rate zero.

q: Which of the following is the BEST example of a heterozygous condition:
a: the matching alleles for a certain physical characteristic are different
one of a pair of chromosomes is lost
e: A heterozygous trait means having two different genetic instructions, like getting one brown-eyed allele and one blue-eyed allele.

q: Which of the following pairs of structures can be considered homologous [hoe-MAWL-uh-gus]?
e: A human hand and a cat paw share the exact same bone blueprint, like secret family cousins wearing different gloves.

q: Which of the following is NOT a baleen whale?
e: While baleen whales use giant hairy strainers to catch snacks, pilot whales smile with a mouth full of real teeth!

q: Where would you find squalene?
a: In the head of a sperm whale
In the intestines of a sperm whale
In the liver of a shark
In the stomach of a shark
e: Sharks pack lightweight squalene oil inside their big livers, helping them float like magic through the deep blue ocean.

q: Which of the following parts of a cell is most directly responsible for synthesizing proteins:
e: Think of ribosomes as bustling little factory workers, stitching tiny parts together to assemble all the cell's essential proteins!

q: Arginine [AHR-juh-neen] is a positively charged amino acid in water. This amino acid is considered which of the following?
e: Arginine holds onto a positive charge in water, which proudly earns it a spot in the basic amino acid club.

q: Chromosomes are composed of:
e: Chromosomes are neat little packages where your long recipe of DNA stays tidily wrapped around spools of protein.

q: Which of the following is the primary function of vascular tissue in plants:
e: Plant vascular tissue works like a bundle of drinking straws, happily carrying water and sweet juices up and down.

q: In which of the following cells would myelin most likely be found:
e: Myelin wraps around long neurons like a snug winter coat, helping thoughts and signals zoom through your nerves.

q: In which of the following environments would a thermophilic bacteria most likely evolve:
e: Thermophilic bacteria adore bubbling heat, making a cozy hot spring their absolute favorite place to grow and thrive.

q: Which of the following is a general term widely used by scientists to indicate artificial growth of cells in the laboratory:
e: When scientists give tiny cells a cozy dish and warm broth to multiply in a lab, they call it a culture!

q: Which of the following is an example of chemosynthesis?
a: A Venus flytrap breaking down the phosphates in a fly
A plant obtaining fixated nitrogen from bacteria rich soil
Prokaryotes [proh-KAR-ee-ohts] obtaining energy from sulfur compounds from the sea vents on the ocean floor
A human being breaking down vitamins and minerals for metabolic digestion
e: Deep in the pitch-black ocean, tiny microbes make chemosynthesis magic by turning harsh vent chemicals into tasty meals without sunlight.

q: A small population of native red-backed salamanders is migrating downhill towards a vernal pool. Along the way, half of the population is lost while crossing a road. This would possibly lead to which of the following outcomes?
a: More competition among members of the population
Stationary individuals that do not migrate to vernal pools
e: Losing salamanders to pure bad luck is genetic drift, which accidentally changes what family traits the survivors pass on.

q: Which species of tuna is in immediate danger of extinction due to overfishing?
e: Fast-swimming southern bluefin tuna are so heavily fished that these majestic ocean speedsters are in danger of disappearing completely.

q: Which of the following plants traps and digests insects:
e: A sundew plant sparkles with sweet, sticky drops that trick curious bugs, gluing them tight so it can digest them.

q: Which of the following is the most important function of fiber tracheids [tray-key-ids] in woody plants?
a: Absorption of nutrients from the soil
e: These sturdy plant fibers act like wooden beams inside a house, keeping giant trees standing tall and proud!

q: Mercury and some other toxins have the ability to bioaccumulate in higher trophic levels. This is partially due to the fact that these toxins are soluble in which of the following?
e: Sneaky toxins melt right into an animal's body fat, hiding there safely instead of washing away.

q: Which of the following junctions forms a water-tight seal?
e: Adherent junctions act like waterproof glue, zipping cells tightly together so not a single drop leaks past.

q: Which of the following terms is most often used to describe a biochemical reaction where the forward reaction is at the same rate as the reverse reaction:
e: When forward and backward changes march at the exact same speed, the reaction balances happily in chemical equilibrium.

q: Which of the following is an example of metamorphosis?
a: A rabbit giving birth to eight young
A bumble bee larva forming a pupa and emerging as a mature adult
A baby bird emerging from the egg
A stink bug transitioning through multiple instars eventually becoming a mature adult
e: Metamorphosis is nature's ultimate costume change, like a squishy bee larva tucked in its pupa until it sprouts wings and buzzes out.

q: Which of the following is found in both prokaryotic [PRO-care-ee-AW-tic] and eukaryotic [YOU-care-ee-AW-tic] cells?
e: Every living cell needs protein factories to survive, so little ribosomes show up in both simple and complex cells.

q: Which of the following is NOT an accurate representation of cladograms?
a: They emphasize the sequence in which derived characteristics arose
They illustrate the benefits provided by the derived characteristic
They visually organize the relationships between organisms that share characteristics
They can be constructed for any group of organisms
e: Cladograms map out how cousins are related, but they don't explain whether a trait actually helps a creature survive.

q: In a heart transplant patient, which of the following cells causes transplant rejection by attacking the heart?
e: Overprotective T cells spot the borrowed heart, mistakenly see it as an enemy invader, and launch an attack.

q: Which of the following statements regarding corals and zooxanthellae [zoh-uh-zan-THEL-ee] is FALSE?
a: Corals can live for a few months without their zooxanthellae
When a coral bleaches the zooxanthellae die
The color of a coral tissue is largely due to the zooxanthellae
Increased water temperature can prompt a bleaching event
e: Stressed corals do not kill their algae partners during bleaching; they just evict them into the water, hoping to reunite later.

q: The development of polyploidy in plants plays the most direct role in which of the following?
e: In sympatric speciation, plants duplicate their DNA sets and instantly blossom into brand-new species right beside their plant neighbors.

q: Which of the following is likely to occur when applying water or heat from an iron to reversibly straighten hair?
e: Warm water or a hot iron gently unzips weak hydrogen bonds holding hair keratin together, letting bouncy curls relax flat.

q: When using the gel electrophoresis technique, which of the following DNA segments will migrate the furthest from where they were loaded?
e: In this gooey obstacle race, the smallest DNA pieces easily slip through tiny spaces and zoom the farthest!

q: Plastids surrounded by a double membrane are evidence for what?
e: Like packing a lunch inside a lunchbox, secondary endosymbiosis happened when one cell swallowed another, wrapping it in two cozy protective blankets.

q: What is the ultimate purpose of the Calvin cycle?
a: To convert carbon dioxide into sugars
To convert waste products to oxygen
To convert sugars, fatty acids, and amino acids into ATP
To separate water into hydrogen and oxygen
e: Inside green leaves, this clever cycle catches invisible carbon dioxide from the air and bakes it into sweet, energizing sugars.

q: Bacteria are more likely used to produce which of the following:
e: Tiny, hardworking bacteria happily gobble up alcohol and turn it into the tangy, sour vinegar we splash on salads!

q: Which of the following accounts for the largest increase in cancer death rate in the USA between the years 1900 and 1990:
e: As smoking became very popular during the twentieth century, lung cancer tragically saw the biggest rise in deaths.

q: Which of the following parts of a fish can be used to estimate its age?
e: Just like tree trunks, a fish's scales grow tiny rings each year that reveal its secret age.

q: Which of the following statements is NOT true about emphysema?
a: Emphysema makes people progressively shorter of breath
Smoking is the leading cause of emphysema
Pulmonary rehabilitation can reverse the damage from emphysema
Pneumothorax [noo-muh-THOHR-aks] is a possible complication of emphysema
e: Special breathing exercises help folks stay active, but they cannot magically rebuild the lung tissue emphysema has already damaged.

q: Prokaryotic cells divide by the process of:
e: Simple prokaryotes make new friends through binary fission, copying their insides and neatly pinching into two identical twins.

q: What type of animal tissue is found in the ears and nose as structural support?
e: Bendy, rubbery cartilage gives your nose and ears their springy shape so you can wiggle them without snapping bone.

q: In what cellular component does a plant cell store water?
e: Think of the central vacuole as a giant, thirsty water balloon inside the plant cell, keeping everything fresh and crisp.

q: Of the following, which level of taxonomic classification is the most specific?
e: Out of this group, a family is the tightest circle of relatives, sorting living things far more specifically than orders or classes.

q: Which of the following is the correct botanical term for the stem of a flower:
e: A peduncle is the strong green stalk that proudly lifts a flower up to greet the warm sun.

q: In healthy mammals, which of the following is least likely to be filtered out of the bloodstream by the glomerulus [glo-MAIR-yoo-lus]?
e: Albumin is like a giant beach ball, far too big to squeeze through the kidney's tiny filter holes! It stays happily inside your blood.

q: In humans, chemical digestion of protein does NOT occur in which of the following areas?
e: Your mouth loves chomping food and breaking down sugars, but chemical protein digestion must wait until your stomach wakes up!

q: Which of the following is NOT found in an animal cell?
e: Animal cells stay squishy and flexible so creatures can move, leaving rigid cell walls to the stiff stems of plants.

q: Which of the following describes the shape of a bacterial pilus:
e: A bacterial pilus acts like a super-thin hollow tube, reaching out like a tiny straw to grab onto things.

q: What portion of the human digestive system is responsible for nearly all nutrient absorption?
e: Despite its humble name, your long, winding small intestine is the superstar that absorbs almost every yummy nutrient from your food.

q: Digestion begins in the mouth because saliva contains salivary amylase [AM-ill-ace]. What macromolecule does amylase digest?
e: Amylase in your spit acts like hungry little scissors, quickly chopping giant starchy pretzels into tiny, sweet bits.

q: Which scientist is credited with discovering cells?
e: Robert Hooke peeked through his microscope at cork and discovered tiny empty rooms he named cells!

q: What environmental condition is mandatory for yeast to complete fermentation?
e: Yeast only kicks off its bubbling fermentation magic when there is zero oxygen around for it to breathe.

q: Which of the following is the botanical term for the haploid generation in moss plants:
e: That soft green carpet of moss in the woods is the gametophyte stage, proudly carrying one set of genes.

q: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of bacteria?
e: Little bacteria keep their DNA floating freely inside because they do not have a cozy home called a nucleus.

q: Which of the following is the general relationship between the availability of soil nutrients and bacterial populations?
a: Increased bacterial populations are predicted as soil nutrients increase
Decreased bacterial populations are predicted as soil nutrients increase
Bacterial populations are not impacted by nutrient availability
There are no bacteria in soil
e: When soil is loaded with tasty nutrients, hungry little bacteria throw a feast and multiply like crazy!

q: Which of the following cell types undergo meiosis?
e: A primary spermatocyte gets ready to make future sperm by dividing through meiosis, shuffling genes into brand-new cells.

q: A scientist performs a Gram stain on an unknown strain of bacteria and observes that the bacteria are stained purple. What does this indicate about the bacteria?
a: Their nuclei are high in collagen
Their cell walls contain large amounts of peptidoglycan
Their cell walls are surrounded by lipotoxins
e: That lovely purple color means these tiny critters wear thick jackets made of peptidoglycan, soaking up dye like a sponge.

q: Which of the following is the least likely to be a characteristic of an invasive species?
a: It will only survive under a narrow range of environmental conditions
It will have a longer reproductive cycle than native species
It will do economic and/or environmental harm in a new environment
e: Invasive invaders love exploring everywhere, so they rarely limit themselves to a fussy, narrow set of living conditions.

q: In humans, olfactory receptors are primarily located in which of the following locations?
e: Up inside your nose, special olfactory receptors wait like eager detectives to sniff out smells from warm cookies to stinky socks.

q: Which of the following types of diversity is the most difficult to effectively and sustainably improve?
e: Rebuilding a whole ecosystem means balancing countless plants, animals, soil, and weather, making ecosystem diversity the hardest to restore.

q: Which of the following is a central mechanism for homeostasis in which the product of a metabolic or physiological pathway regulates its production by inhibiting an earlier step in its own production?
e: Like a smart heater clicking off when a room gets warm, negative feedback stops a pathway once enough is made.

q: Which of the following animal products has NOT been correctly paired with the animal that produces it?
e: Woolly sheep make soft, waterproof lanolin wax to keep their coats dry, not goats!

q: Which of the following is the best reason that snakes do not reproduce with worms?
e: Mechanical isolation simply means their body parts do not fit together, like trying to plug a garden hose into a keyhole.

q: A nucleotide contains all except which of the following?
e: Amino acids belong to proteins, so DNA's tiny building blocks leave them out of their special three-part recipe.

q: Which of the following is an example of anaerobic respiration?
a: Yeast performing fermentation to release ethyl alcohol and carbon dioxide
A rose using carbon dioxide to produce glucose in the Calvin cycle
A mouse cell using one molecule of glucose to produce 36 ATPs
A plant performing photosynthesis to produce energy for storage
e: Hungry yeast can feast without any oxygen, burping out alcohol and carbon dioxide through anaerobic fermentation.

q: During which of the following phases of meiosis [my-OH-sis] do homologous [ha-MAWL-uh-gus] chromosomes break apart?
e: In Anaphase I, matching chromosome partners share a gentle goodbye tug and pull apart toward opposite ends of the cell.

q: Muscle cells in our heart are constantly working. Which of the following organelles would they have in larger quantities than other cells in the body?
e: Because your heart beats non-stop, its cells are packed with extra mitochondria, the bustling power plants making endless energy!

q: Which of the following will most likely occur for a bacteria that is an obligate or strict anaerobe (read as: an-AYE-robe) when grown in a test tube of nutrient agar that remains undisturbed :
a: the bacteria only grow against the walls of the test tube
the bacteria only grow at the top of the test tube
the bacteria only grow at the bottom of the test tube
e: These shy germs run away from fresh air, nestling down at the very bottom of the tube where no oxygen can bother them.

q: Which of the following is NOT an example of an angiosperm [AN-jee-uh-spurm]?
e: Douglas firs make woody pinecones instead of flowers and fruit, which means they are gymnosperms, not angiosperms.

q: Indoleacetic acid is the most common of what group of hormones?
e: Indoleacetic acid belongs to the auxin family, the plant whisperers that tell growing green stems to reach for the sun.

q: The majority of ocean organisms living in hydrothermal vents are believed to be which of the following?
e: Down in the pitch-black deep sea, trillions of super-tough bacteria happily feast on hot chemicals where almost nothing else can survive.

q: You press down on your arm and feel a pulse beating. From which of the following types of blood vessels is the pulse originating?
e: Every heartbeat sends a powerful rush of blood through your stretchy arteries, which you can feel dancing right under your fingertips!

q: The extinction of large hooved mammals from Central America has been implicated in the reduction of what types of plants, which relied on them for seed dispersal?
a: Plants with pods, such as peas
e: Ancient giant beasts were the only critters big enough to gulp down massive avocado pits and plant them everywhere.

q: Which of the following is the location of the human thymus gland:
e: Tucked right behind your breastbone in your upper chest, this cozy little gland trains brave defender cells to protect you.

q: Imagine you are dropped at a random place on planet Earth. You are not told where you are. However, you are told that the average temperature here is 78 Fahrenheit and that over 180 inches of rain fall here every year. In what kind of biome do you most likely find yourself?
e: Tropical rain forests stay delightfully warm and get drenched in non-stop showers, making them the wettest, coziest spots on Earth.

q: Which of the following would be most effective for treating a human collagen deficiency?
e: Your body needs vitamin C like a cheerful master builder, using it to glue your tissues together with strong collagen.

q: Which of the following is the BEST description of the primary function of a protein enzyme:
a: a catalyst made of amino acids
a string of amino acids added to a sugar to make the sugar stronger
as a short term form of energy storage
e: Built from amino acids, an enzyme acts like a speedy helper called a catalyst, zipping up chemical reactions inside your body.

q: In what state will a plant cell be if placed in a hypotonic [high-poh-tawnic] environment?
e: Water rushes inside like air into a balloon, puffing the plant cell up nice and firm in a state called turgor.

q: Hormones released by the posterior pituitary control numerous emotions, drives, and autonomic functions. In which of the following locations are those hormones actually produced?
e: The wise hypothalamus acts like a master chef, whipping up hormones before sending them to the pituitary for delivery.

q: A glacier splits a population of rabbits in two. Which of the following best describes what might happen in the two populations over a long period of time?
e: When an icy glacier separates rabbit families, allopatric speciation takes over as the two groups slowly evolve into different species.

q: Which of the following statements best describes the primary difference between animal centrosomes and plant centrosomes?
a: Plant centrosomes have a rough exterior made of cellulose
Plant centrosomes do not have centrioles
Animal centrosomes are in the cytoplasm
e: While animal centrosomes use tiny barrel-shaped helpers called centrioles, plant centrosomes cleverly organize cell division completely without them.

q: Transgenic animals carry the genes from other species in their DNA through a deliberate modification of their genome. Which of the following phrases does NOT reflect why transgenic animals are currently being produced in the United States?
a: To have animal models for human diseases
To test the purity of human proteins (such as human insulin) used as drugs
For the production of human food
e: While transgenic critters help scientists test medicines and study diseases, they are not made to fill our dinner plates with food.

q: Which of the following is not an ectotherm?
e: Playful otters make their own toasty body heat to stay warm in cold water, so they are not cold-blooded ectotherms.

q: Which of the following is NOT a mechanism plants use to disperse their seeds?
e: Apomixis is a clever way plants create seeds without pollen, not a travel plan to scatter them across the meadow!

q: Which of the following is NOT a rodent:
e: Even with their twitchy noses, rabbits are lagomorphs, not rodents, because they pack an extra pair of upper chewing teeth!

q: Which of the following exhibits quaternary [QUAH-tur-nairee] protein structure?
