e: Hemoglobin has quaternary structure because four protein teammates clasp together like a squad to carry oxygen through your blood.

q: Plant metabolism must:
a: Produce carbon dioxide and consume oxygen
Neither produce nor consume carbon dioxide or oxygen
Consume carbon dioxide and produce oxygen
Both produce and consume carbon dioxide and oxygen
e: Plants make and use both oxygen and carbon dioxide, balancing making food in sunshine with breathing day and night.

q: Which of the following is NOT a main class of connective tissue in humans?
e: While every tissue is packed with cells, cellular is just a description, not a main connective tissue group like bone or cartilage.

q: Unlike other mollusks , cephalopods (read as: SEH-fah-loh- pohds) have which of the following characteristics?
e: Speedy octopuses pump their blue blood safely through tidy, closed pipes instead of letting it slosh around loosely.

q: You are looking through a microscope at an unlabeled sample of human tissue. You notice the tissue is multinucleated, and contains striations. What tissue are you examining?
e: Striped and packed with many nuclei, skeletal muscles are the mighty tissue helping your bones run and jump!

q: Which of the following cells stimulate macrophages, B cells, and T cells?
e: Helper T cells act like cheerful team captains, rallying macrophages, B cells, and other T cells to join the big germ-fighting squad.

q: Although not scientifically verified, which of the following plant communities has been hypothesized to utilize allelopathy?
e: Tough chaparral shrubs might use allelopathy, leaking secret chemicals into the dirt to stop neighboring seeds from crowding their sunny space.

q: Which of the following fix nitrogen in soil?
e: Friendly legumes team up with helpful root bacteria to turn air into rich soil food!

q: If you eat a tuna fish sandwich, which of the following types of fish would you be eating?
e: Tuna zoom through the water with fins supported by webs of tiny bony rods, making them super-fast ray-finned fish!

q: DNA ligase [LYE-gase] is an enzyme that catalyzes which of the following reactions?
e: DNA ligase acts like tiny magical glue, building phosphodiester bonds to stitch broken strands neatly back together.

q: Which of the following is the scientific name for the part of the human brain where higher brain operations occur such as thinking, imagination, mathematical reasoning and language:
e: Your wrinkly cerebral cortex is the master control room where your deepest thoughts, bright daydreams, and clever ideas come alive.

q: Which of the following is an example of a frameshift mutation?
a: Adding one nucleotide in the middle of a gene
Deleting three nucleotides in the middle of a gene
Adding three nucleotides in the middle of a gene
e: Slipping a single extra letter into the gene scrambles every three-letter word after it, shifting the whole recipe out of line.

q: Name the tiny air sacs involved in the exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide in the lungs.
e: Millions of tiny alveoli act like microscopic balloons, happily trading fresh oxygen for carbon dioxide every time you take a breath!

q: In which of the following situations would it be most helpful for a patient to take an antihistamine?
a: After getting scratched by a rusty nail
e: Antihistamines calm your body down when allergies make you sneeze and itch over harmless specks of pollen!

q: Which of the following statements is TRUE regarding heterochromatin [hetero- CROW-ma-tin]?
a: It consists of DNA loosely wound around histones
During mitosis [my-TOW-sis], most nuclear DNA is found as heterochromatin
Chromatin [CROW-mah-tin] organization is determined by DNA modifications
e: When a cell divides in mitosis, its DNA neatly packs into super-tight bundles called heterochromatin for safe travel.

q: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of the bald eagle?
a: They have both binocular and peripheral vision
They only eat animals they capture themselves
They are thought to mate for life
They tend to construct their nests near water
e: Majestic bald eagles love easy meals, happily snatching snacks from other birds or scavenging leftovers instead of always hunting fresh prey.

q: Which of the following terms is MOST commonly used to refer to the copying of DNA during the cell cycle:
e: Before a growing cell divides, it photocopies its precious genetic recipe book through a process called replication.

q: The seed coat of angiosperm seeds typically develops from which of the following?
e: The plant wraps its tiny baby in protective layers called integuments, which toughen up into a snug little coat.

q: In the human body, the gallbladder is in immediate proximity to what organ?
e: Your little gallbladder snuggles right beneath the big liver, gladly catching and storing its digestive juices.

q: Which of the following leukocytes [LOO-kuh-sits] occurs in the LEAST abundance in the healthy human body?
e: Basophils are the rarest defenders in your bloodstream, making up less than one percent of your whole white blood cell team.

q: Which of the following represents the primary symptom from the chytrid fungus infecting amphibians?
a: The fungus attacks the skin, making respiration difficult
The fungal spores enter through the eyes, causing permanent blindness
The fungus is ingested and produces repeated regurgitation followed by death
e: Frogs need soft skin to breathe, so this unkind fungus thickens their outer coat until taking a breath becomes terribly hard.

q: The cardiac center is located in which of the following structures?
e: Tucked at the brain's base, the marvelous medulla quietly works day and night to keep your beating heart on beat.

q: Which of the following is NOT a cause of microevolution?
e: When creatures pick partners completely at random, gene mixes stay nicely balanced instead of shifting over time.

q: Which of the following chemical bonds is most important in DNA secondary structure?
e: Gentle hydrogen bonds hold DNA's twisting ladder together, acting like tiny magnetic hands that can unzip and zip right back up!

q: Which of the following best describes how fungi feed?
a: Some are photoautotrophs, while others are chemoautotrophs
e: Fungi are heterotrophs because they cannot whip up food from sunshine, so they happily absorb tasty nutrients from their surroundings.

q: Which of the following is the BEST example of how evolution progresses:
a: animals learn to survive through experience and teach their offspring
certain mutations improve an organism's offspring's chances to survive and reproduce in different environments
animals develop certain strengths and weaknesses through experience and pass the knowledge down by example
an animal that is successful at hunting will be more likely to survive
e: Helpful genetic changes give baby creatures special superpowers to survive tough challenges and pass those gifts to their own young!

q: Some scientists believe that humans have possibly caused the sixth mass extinction on Earth. Which of the following is a major consequence of mass extinction?
a: Stabilizing population flux within a specific environment
e: When a mass extinction strikes, countless species vanish forever, leading to a huge loss of Earth's marvelous biodiversity.

q: In which part of the plant would you expect to find the largest concentration of photosynthetic pigments?
e: Leaves are a plant's sun-catching solar panels, packed with green pigments to soak up all the light they can!

q: Which of the following animals is most closely related in phylogeny [fye-LAW-jen-ee] to a slug?
e: Believe it or not, the octopus is a soft-bodied mollusk cousin to the slug, just swimming with eight arms instead!

q: Sharks do not have a swim bladder. What major organ controls buoyancy in sharks?
e: A shark stays afloat with a giant liver packed with light, buoyant oil, like wearing built-in water wings!

q: Sharks have repeated rows of identical teeth that are shed throughout their lives. Which of the following best categorizes their teeth?
e: Because every single chomper in a shark's grin shares the exact same pointy shape, they are called homodont teeth.

q: Which of the following is the causative agent for some cases of familial fatal insomnia, Creutzfeld-Jacob disease, and kuru?
e: A prion is a misfolded protein that acts like a copycat bully, reshaping healthy brain proteins and causing serious disease.

q: Which of the following ocean organisms is the predator of an oyster?
e: A sea star hugs an oyster tight with tiny tube feet, prying its shell open for a tasty seabed snack.

q: Which of the following is considered the dominant generation in flowering plants:
e: The leafy green plant you see blooming outside is the sporophyte stage, ruling as the main, dominant form of a flower's life!

q: Which of the following do clams use as an anchor to fix themselves into the sand:
e: A clam stretches out its squishy muscular foot to dig deep into wet sand and anchor itself safely from rolling waves!

q: Which of the following human organs has the largest mass?
e: Like two giant, spongy balloons filling your chest, your lungs weigh much more than smaller neighbors like the kidneys or pancreas.

q: Which of the following animals has the longest gestation period?
e: Mother elephants carry their gigantic, cuddly calves for nearly two whole years before welcoming them into the sunny world.

q: Which of the following organisms has spines?
e: A sea urchin protects its soft round body with a prickly coat of sharp, movable spines that ward off hungry neighbors!

q: Which of the following errors in human meiosis would LEAST likely affect the resulting offspring?
a: Gene duplication in a transcriptionally-silent region of the chromosome
Gene duplication in a transcriptionally-active region of the chromosome
e: Because that quiet part of the chromosome is sleeping and turned off, making extra copies causes no trouble at all.

q: A nonsense mutation is most likely to result in which of the following events?
e: A nonsense mutation shouts stop too early, cutting the growing protein short before it can finish its grand adventure.

q: Pellagra [puh-LAG-ruh] results from a deficiency of what?
e: Our bodies need vitamin B3 to stay energized, so missing this vital nutrient causes an uncomfortable illness called pellagra.

q: Which of the following was a top predator during the Devonian period?
e: Dunkleosteus was a mighty ancient fish wearing heavy armor that ruled Devonian seas like a giant underwater king with bone-snapping jaws!

q: Chromosomal polyploidy results in which of the following phenotypic differences in fruits and vegetables?
e: Packing extra sets of chromosomes makes plant cells puff up like balloons, adding serious weight to your favorite juicy fruits.

q: An organism's way of life, including its habitat, food, predators, and other organisms it competes with for resources make up an organism's:
e: An animal's special job, home, and daily routine fit together like a puzzle piece called its ecological niche.

q: In human nerves, the nerve impulse or message occurs primarily because of the movement of ions of what two elements across the cell membranes of nerves:
e: Tiny sodium and potassium particles dance across cell doorways, passing tiny sparks to send messages through your nerves.

q: Which of the following pairs is NOT a correct matching of an organism with its external symmetry classification?
e: Lobsters have matching left and right halves, which makes them bilateral, not biradial like comb jellies.

q: The malleus, incus, and stapes [STAY-peez] are small bones that play a role in which of the following functions?
e: These three teeny ear bones dance together, bouncing sound vibrations deep inside so you can hear every lovely song!

q: Stromatolites [stroh-MAT-oh-lite] have been used to study the age of which of the following?
e: Stromatolites are rocky castles built by microscopic critters billions of years ago, showing us what Earth's very first life looked like.

q: Which of the following infectious diseases cannot be cured with current antibiotics:
e: Antibiotics only zap pesky bacteria, so they cannot cure influenza, which is caused by a sneaky virus instead.

q: You are using a light microscope to look at cells stained with a dye that detects chromatin [KROH-mah-tin] and can see densely-colored regions that you recognize as chromosomes. Which of the following must be true?
e: DNA only packs into tidy, visible chromosome bundles when a cell is ready to divide in mitosis!

q: Ribosomes are made of:
e: Ribosomes are tiny kitchen helpers built from nucleic acids and proteins, working side by side to cook up fresh cell recipes.

q: What happens to the population of white blood cells when a bacterial infection occurs?
e: Your body sounds the alarm and rushes out whole armies of brave white blood cells to battle the invading germs!

q: During which stage of mitosis do the chromosomes line up in the center of the nucleus?
e: In metaphase, chromosomes shuffle like dancers into a neat, straight line right across the middle of the cell.

q: Which is NOT one of the essential activities that occurs in the digestive process?
e: Your tummy absorbs nutrients inside, but adsorption just means sticking to an outside surface, so it is not part of digestion.

q: What is the correct term for a marine organism whose internal salt concentration varies with that of their environment?
e: Instead of fighting the salty sea, easygoing osmoconformers simply match their inside saltiness to the water around them!

q: Which of the following statements is NOT true about the plant Mimosa pudica [mee-MO-suh POO-dee-kuh]?
a: Its leaves fold inward and droop when it is touched or shaken
Aqueous [AY-kwee-uhs] extracts of its roots inhibit cobra venom
e: This shy little plant actually began its journey in the Americas, not Africa, where it first learned to fold up its leaves.

q: Hormones regulate the concentration of glucose in the blood. Which of the following hormones is properly described by its role in this regulation?
a: Epinephrine [e-puh-NE-fruhn] suppresses release of glucagon [GLOO-kuh-gon] and insulin
Somatostatin [suh-mat-uh-STAT-in] enhances release of glucose from glycogen
e: Insulin acts like a gentle key, unlocking cells so sugar moves inside, which safely decreases blood glucose levels.

q: Kate is constructing a cladogram [KLAD-oh-gram] that includes angiosperms, conifers, ferns, and mosses. Which of the following is most likely to be an ancestral trait of this cladogram?
e: All these green plant buddies stand up tall using stems, an ancient trait they shared way before flowers or seeds ever appeared.

q: The skull of a new mammalian species is found and all of the teeth are sharp and angled. Based on this data, which of the following is the most reasonable conclusion?
e: Those dagger-sharp teeth were made for slicing meat, proving this creature was definitely a hungry carnivore.

q: Which of the following structures is too small to be seen reliably with a basic light microscope with a 400-times objective?
e: A viral capsid is so teeny-tiny that regular light microscopes cannot spot it without special superpower lenses.

q: Epiphytes [EP-uh-fyts] primarily obtain water and nutrients through what?
e: Living high up on tree branches, epiphytes drink rain and catch nutrients directly through their thirsty leaves.

q: Lipids will dissolve best in which of the following:
e: Greasy fats and water just refuse to get along, but chloroform welcomes oily lipids with open arms and dissolves them easily.

q: Which of the following animals are believed to be the closest living relatives to the dinosaurs:
e: Crocodiles and dinosaurs share the same ancient reptile family branch, making these toothy river giants their closest cousins alive today.

q: Which of the following organisms is probably the most commonly studied prokaryote?
e: Meet E. coli, the most famous bacterium on Earth! Curious scientists have studied this little swimmer more than any other prokaryote.

q: The difference between xylem [ZY-luhm] and phloem [FLOH-em] is which of the following?
a: Xylem transports water and dissolved nutrients, while phloem transports dissolved organic materials in an aqueous solution [AK-wee-uhs]
Phloem transports water and minerals, while xylem transports sugars
Phloem is not found in plants, while xylem is only present in plants
Xylem is not found in plants, while phloem is only present in plants
e: Xylem sips water upward from thirsty roots, while phloem delivers delicious, sugary snacks to every corner of the plant.

q: Which of the following portions of the small intestine receives food directly from the stomach?
e: The duodenum is the very first stretch of the small intestine, welcoming dinner the second it tumbles out of the stomach.

q: Gary the gardener raises a species of annual flowers that can produce pink or white flowers. Gary buys a pot of white flowers and plants them in his garden and each successive year saves only that year's generation of seeds to plant the next year. Over many generations of years of flowers Gary only ever sees white flowers. Which of the following is the BEST explanation for this breeding pattern:
a: the original plant was homozygous dominant
the original plant was homozygous recessive
the original plant was heterozygous for both colors
the original plant was homozygous but Gary cannot know for sure whether it is a dominant or recessive color
e: The plant was homozygous because it only made white seeds, but without pink flowers to compare, Gary cannot know which color dominates.

q: Which of the following structures would likely be the most resistant to heat denaturation?
e: A bacterial endospore is like a sleeping germ inside heat-proof armor, built tough to survive boiling temperatures without melting.

q: Most nerves in mammals are covered with a sheath of myelin [MY-ah-lin]. Which of the following is the main function of this layer?
e: This cozy myelin blanket wraps around nerves like a slick slide, helping electrical messages zip across your body in a flash!

q: Which of the following kinds of microscopes typically is used to view the surface of objects ranging in size from cells to small insects like fleas to reveal minute surface details:
e: A scanning electron microscope bounces beams of tiny particles off flea coats to reveal unbelievable, 3D surface details!

q: Which of the following hormones induces glucose uptake by cells after food consumption?
e: After you eat, insulin acts like a friendly doorman, unlocking your cells so sweet sugar can step inside and fuel you up.

q: Suppose your biological mother has blood type A and your biological father has blood type AB. Which of the following is definitely NOT your blood type?
e: Dad has genes for A and B, so he always passes one along, meaning a baby can never end up with type O!

q: Which of the following do all chordates possess at some time in their lives:
e: Long before they grow up, all chordates share a secret badge of honor: tiny gill slits tucked along their necks!

q: Which of the following membrane transport methods is most important for release of neurotransmitters like acetylcholine during synaptic signaling?
e: In exocytosis, tiny bubbles fuse with the cell's outer wall to politely deliver chemical messages to their neighbors.

q: If you touched a crawfish, you would notice that its body is hard. That is because the crawfish:
e: A crawfish wears its hard bones on the outside like a crunchy suit of knightly armor, called an exoskeleton.

q: What structures on the outside of bacteria are MOST typically associated with the ability of bacteria to control their movement:
e: Flagella act like little motorboat propellers, spinning around to steer a tiny bacterium on its grand adventures.

q: Which of the following kingdoms contains organisms that directly produce methane as a byproduct of metabolism?
e: Ancient, tough little microbes called archaea love burping out stinky methane gas as they turn their food into energy!

q: Which of the following best describes the relationship between epiphytes and the trees they live on?
e: In commensalism, epiphytes perch happily on tree branches to catch sunlight without bothering or harming their hosts at all.

q: The first evidence that nitrogen-fixing bacteria populations have become too low in a terrestrial biome would be a decline in which of the following populations?
e: Plants are producers that crave nitrogen, so without helpful bacteria around, our leafy green friends dwindle first.

q: The antibiotic penicillin halts bacterial growth by doing which of the following?
a: Interfering with the synthesis of the bacterial cell wall
Interfering with the synthesis of bacterial ribosomes
Preventing attachment of messenger RNA to the ribosome
e: Penicillin stops sneaky bacteria from building their tough outer cell walls, leaving them defenseless and unable to grow.

q: Pyrimidines are important components in nucleic acids, vitamins, drugs, and many other compounds. Which of the following nucleotide bases is NOT a pyrimidine?
e: Adenine is a double-ringed purine, standing tall beside the smaller, single-ring pyrimidines like a proud big brother.

q: Which of the following statements is NOT true about botulism?
a: It is caused by a virus
Food-borne botulism can thrive in raw honey
Its toxin can be used to reduce severe underarm sweating
e: Botulism is not caused by a virus, but by a crafty little bacterium that makes a powerful toxin.

q: Which of the following types of nucleic acid carries a complementary copy of a gene from the DNA to the cytoplasm to instruct the order in which amino acids will be made into a protein:
e: Messenger RNA acts like a cheerful mail carrier, delivering precious recipe copies from cozy DNA right out to the cell's protein kitchen!

q: Which of the following nitrogenous bases is the most structurally similar to guanine?
e: Guanine and adenine are purines, sharing a two-ring structure that makes them look like close chemical cousins.

q: Which of the following animals completes a round-trip migration over several generations?
e: Tiny globe skimmer dragonflies treat migration like a family relay race, letting their children and grandchildren finish the epic round trip.

q: Cheese, yogurt, apple cider, olives, and sauerkraut are all made with:
e: Friendly bacteria are tiny kitchen helpers that feast on foods, transforming milk into tangy yogurt and tasty cheese!

q: What is the name of the bone in the human chin?
e: Your mandible is the mighty lower jawbone that lets you chew, talk, and show off your chin.

q: An adaptation is any kind of modification in bodily structure or behavior that increases an organism's chance of survival in their environment. Which of the following is NOT an example of an adaptation in an organism to its current environment?
a: The large eyes of an owl for improved night vision
The spines of a cactus for improved water retention
The appendix of a human for improved protein digestion
The jaws of a Venus Flytrap for improved ability to capture insects
e: Your appendix does not digest protein today, so it is just a quiet leftover rather than a helpful modern survival tool.

q: Which of the following types of joints can be found in the knuckles of a human index finger?
e: Your index knuckle is an ellipsoid joint, letting your finger happily wave up, down, and side to side.

q: During what period are the first reptiles thought to have emerged?
e: In the swampy, giant-tree forests of the Carboniferous period, the very first scaly reptiles made their grand entrance onto land!

q: Which of the following molecules is most commonly used for the transport of energy in cells?
e: Think of ATP as a rechargeable battery, zooming around inside cells to deliver power everywhere it is needed!

q: Which of the following are homologous structures:
a: wing of a bat and the arm of a human
leg of a cat and the wing of a fly
stinger of a bee and the fang of a snake
rattler of a rattle snake and the whistle of a song bird
e: A bat wing and a human arm share the exact same bone blueprint, just cleverly reshaped for soaring or waving.

q: Which of the following best describes the role of most white blood cells?
e: White blood cells are your body’s loyal little security guards, bravely chasing away sneaky germs to lead your immune response.

q: Which of the classes of biomacromolecules has the highest energy density per unit mass?
e: Fats are nature's ultimate energy backpacks, cramming far more fuel into every tiny bite than proteins or carbs can.

q: Which of these constitutes a correct DNA base pairing?
e: Inside our DNA ladder, base A always reaches across to lock hands perfectly with its favorite partner, T.

q: Which of the following types of plant cell tissue is considered most important for structural support?
e: Sclerenchyma cells build extra-tough, woody walls, acting like sturdy wooden beams that keep tall plants standing proud against the wind.

q: Honeybees and other pollinators transfer pollen from the:
a: Anther to the Stigma of the Flower
Stigma to the Anther of the Flower
Filament to the Sepal of the Flower
Sepal to the Filament of the Flower
e: A busy bee dusts yellow powder off the flower's pollen-packed anther and delivers it straight to the sticky stigma next door.

q: Which of the following is the longest snake alive today?
e: Stretching out longer than two tall adults lying head to toe, the reticulated python wins the crown for the longest snake!

q: Which of the following phenomena does NOT contribute to water's ability to move against gravity through a plant's vascular system?
e: While xylem pulls water upward, phloem pressure is busy sending sugary snacks downward, so it cannot lift water up tall trees.

q: In humans, which of the following is the name for the tube that makes up the complete digestive system?
e: From your first crunchy bite to the very end, food travels down one continuous winding highway called the alimentary canal.

q: Given that p equals the frequency of the dominant allele and that q equals the frequency of the recessive allele, which of the following equations does NOT correctly represent a Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium?
a: p2 + 2pq + q2 = (p + q)2 [p squared plus 2 p q plus q squared equals, open parenthesis, p plus q, close parenthesis, squared]
e: Nature balances genes with squared numbers, so the weird scrambled formula 2p + pq + 2q = 1 does not belong.

q: Which of the following terms is used to define benthic organisms that live in the spaces between particles of sediment?
e: Meiofauna are teeny-tiny critters small enough to play hide-and-seek between individual grains of sand on the seafloor.

q: What is the purpose of the lateral line in fish?
e: A fish’s lateral line acts like underwater tickle sensors, feeling hidden vibrations and ripples gliding through the water.

q: Which of the following statements is NOT true about leopards?
a: They are hybrids of lions and panthers
They can leap to the branch of a tree while holding an impala carcass in their mouths
They have a very broad diet
e: Leopards are their own unique wild species, not a mixed-up hybrid of lions and panthers like ancient storytellers once believed.

q: Ferns differ from gymnosperms and angiosperms in which of the following ways?
a: Ferns do not produce seeds, while gymnosperms and angiosperms do
The dominant life stage of ferns is haploid, while gymnosperms and angiosperms are diploid
Ferns do not have non-motile sperm, whereas angiosperms and gymnosperms do
Ferns do not have xylem or phloem [FLOH-em], whereas gymnosperms and angiosperms do
e: Ferns skip making seeds entirely. Instead, these ancient leafy greens spread across the forest floor by floating tiny spores into the wind.

q: Assuming that the following structures are unlabeled and unstained, which would be least likely to be visualized using a light microscope with the standard resolution of 0.2 microns?
e: Ribosomes are far too teeny for standard light microscopes to spot, hiding like microscopic specks inside the cell.

q: Which of the following are the 3 basic organs of higher plants:
e: Every plant relies on roots to drink, stems to stand tall, and leaves to catch warm sunshine.

q: Which of the following groups of organic compounds in the human body are the most diverse in size, shape, and function?
e: Proteins are nature's ultimate shapeshifters, folding into endless forms to tackle almost every job in your body!

q: Which of the following is most likely to be true of a sessile animal?
e: Glued in one spot forever, a sessile creature simply sifts drifting snacks from passing water, making it a filter feeder.

q: You catch a common cold from one of your Science Bowl teammates. Which of the following would be LEAST effective for treating your symptoms?
e: Colds are caused by sneaky viruses, so antibiotics cannot help you because they only battle bacteria!

q: Which of the following locations primarily consists of smooth muscle?
e: Your stomach is made of smooth muscle, gently churning and mashing your lunch without you ever having to think about it.

q: The action of the sodium-potassium pump is an example of which of the following types of transport?
e: Because this tiny cell pump must push substances uphill against the crowd, it burns energy, making it an active transport worker.

q: Which of the following genetic traits would be most expected to increase in prevalence in the population over time?
a: A genetic variant in a deer population that results in a skeletal difference that causes the deer to move more slowly
A genetic variation that leads to behavioral changes due to a decreased fear of predators
A genetic mutation in a mammal that increases the nutrients available in the milk, so that the offspring grow stronger and faster
A genetic mutation that increases the size of the teeth in the mouth, reducing the space available for food in the mouth and eliminating some food choices.
e: Super-nutritious milk helps baby animals grow strong and healthy, making it much easier for them to survive and share that helpful trait!

q: Which of the following fish exhibit protandry and are all male when hatched?
e: Every baby clownfish hatches as a boy, but the bravest leader of the reef can transform into a female later!

q: Which of the following types of interactions will NOT occur between enzymes and their substrates?
e: Enzymes hold their helpers with soft, temporary hugs rather than strong covalent bonds, so they can let go easily.

q: Which of the following molecules gives carrots their orange color?
e: Carotene works like a tiny paintbrush dipped in sunshine, dressing up carrots in their bright orange coats.

q: Which of the following is the MOST common manner for transmission of beef tapeworms to humans:
e: Eating uncooked beef can let hidden tapeworm travelers sneak into a tummy, so cooking meat keeps everyone safe.

q: Keratins are considered structural proteins. This is because they are most often arranged in which of the following shapes:
e: Keratins twist into long, thin fibers, like microscopic ropes braiding together to make tough hair and strong fingernails.

q: Which of the following groups are all invertebrates?
a: Snails, honeybees, sea star, and sea sponges
Grasshoppers, fruit flies, electric eels, and sea horses
e: From squishy snails and bees to sea stars and sponges, none of these little friends have a single backbone!

q: Which of the following is NOT found in both bacterial and human cells?
e: Our cells pack their precious DNA inside a neat little control center called a nucleus, but free-spirited bacteria let theirs wander loose!

q: What is the connective tissue that protects the ends of the bones and allows them to move more easily?
e: Cartilage acts like a slippery, rubbery pillow on bone ends, helping them glide smoothly past each other whenever you wiggle.

q: Which of the following plant groups includes mosses, liverworts, and hornworts?
e: Soft green mosses belong to the bryophyta family, hugging damp rocks like tiny velvet carpets without needing any true roots!

q: Which of the following groups of animals shared the most recent common ancestor with birds?
e: Look closely at a tiny robin and you will see a dinosaur cousin; birds share their most recent family ancestor with prehistoric dinosaurs!

q: Pasteur advanced the understanding of disease through which of the following?
a: Collecting data indicating that viruses can cause disease
Collecting data indicating that bacteria can cause disease
Providing a method to identify pathogens
e: Louis Pasteur gathered clever clues showing that tiny, invisible bacteria are the sneaky troublemakers causing disease.

q: Which of the following is the role of DNA ligase in DNA replication?
a: Joining the 3 prime end of the DNA that replaces the primer to the rest of the sequence
Relieving strain caused by over-winding the DNA strand
e: DNA ligase acts like molecular tape, neatly gluing the newly replaced DNA ends right into the matching genetic strand.

q: Fruit flies are common in homes, restaurants, supermarkets and wherever else fruit is allowed to rot and ferment. Given the opportunity, about how many eggs will a fruit fly lay at a time?
e: One busy little mother fruit fly can fill ripe fruit with about five hundred tiny future babies!

q: Which of the following terms is used to describe the extra copy of a chromosome synthesized during S phase prior to mitosis?
e: When a chromosome makes an identical twin copy of itself, that shiny new partner is called a sister chromatid.

q: How does coral reproduce?
a: It is pollinated by other fish
Eggs and sperm are released in the open water
Male and female coral attract each other
e: Corals throw a giant underwater blizzard party, releasing millions of eggs and sperm to meet and float together on ocean currents!

q: Phosphorus is critical to the formation of nucleic acids, ATP and other energy storing molecules. Where are the largest reservoirs for this important mineral on Earth?
e: Most of Earth's phosphorus is locked deep inside ancient ocean rocks, patiently snoozing under the seafloor for millions of years.

q: Which of the following patterns of inheritance are NOT correctly paired?
a: Red, pink, white color in flowers - sex-linked inheritance
e: Pink snapdragons come from incomplete dominance, not sex-linked traits, blending mom and dad's colors like wet paint.

q: Which of the following classifications would be inclusive of eucalyptus, cattails, duckweed and buttercups?
e: Even tiny duckweed and giant eucalyptus trees are angiosperms, because they all share a secret superpower: making blossoms to show off their seeds.

q: Which of the following organelles would be most abundant in cells that are producing large amounts of ATP through oxidative metabolism:
e: Mitochondria are the mighty powerhouses of the cell, happily churning out energetic ATP sparkplugs to keep things running.

q: In the tri-nomen Canis lupis familiaris, Canis refers to what taxonomic rank?
e: Canis is the genus, a proud group name that packs wolves, jackals, and our favorite pet dogs together like close cousins.

q: The haploidy [HAP-loy-dee] of gametes [GAM-eets] supports which of Gregor Mendel's laws?
e: Gregor Mendel's law of segregation explains how gene pairs split up, ensuring each gamete carries just one copy instead of two.

q: The receptors in the retina of the eye that detect faint light and transfer non-color impulses to the brain are:
e: Night-vision superhero cells called rods help your eyes spot shadowy shapes when the lights go down low!

q: After a forest fire, annual plants will begin growing in the burnt area fairly quickly. Which of the following best explains why?
a: Forest fires do not usually kill all of the local trees
Forest fires expose bare rock, which is a good substrate for annual plant growth
As a climax community, forests cannot be destroyed
Forest fires do not destroy the topsoil, which supports plant growth
e: Even after a roaring blaze, the rich topsoil stays safe below, holding cozy dirt where fresh seeds can quickly sprout.

q: Which of the following types of enzymes would most likely be involved in changing glucose-6-phosphate to glucose-1-phosphate?
e: An isomerase acts like a clever puzzle solver, rearranging the sugar's parts into a new shape without losing a single piece.

q: Which of the following is a major reason for "dead zones" in the ocean?
e: Farm fertilizers wash out to sea, feeding huge algae parties that gobble up all the water's oxygen when they decay.

q: Over hundreds of years, a population of black worms slowly stratifies into a group of ground-dwelling worms and a group of tree-dwelling worms. What type of isolation is observed here?
e: Because some worms chose leafy tree penthouses while others preferred cozy dirt basements, their separate homes kept them apart through habitat isolation.

q: Which of the following kinds of mammal teeth are used to bite and cut?
e: Sitting right up front like sharp little blades, your incisors cleanly snip and cut into crunchy apples every lunchtime.

q: Which of the following species thrives in a mangrove?
e: Mighty alligators love swampy mangroves, gliding smoothly through the warm, tangled tree roots on the hunt.

q: Of the following, which is true of type I diabetes?
a: It most often occurs later in life
It is characterized by the inability of receptors to recognize insulin
It is characterized by the inability of the pancreas to produce insulin
It is most often due to unhealthy lifestyle choices
e: In type one diabetes, the pancreas stops making insulin, the trusty little key needed to unlock sugar for our cells.

q: Cholesterol is responsible for altering membrane fluidity. In which of the following conditions would the presence of cholesterol have the greatest effect on the fluidity of the cell membrane?
a: When cholesterol levels increase and the membrane is at a low temperature
When cholesterol levels increase and the membrane is at a moderate temperature
When cholesterol levels decrease and the membrane is at a low temperature
Cholesterol has the same effect, regardless of the temperature
e: In the chilly cold, membranes want to freeze solid, but extra cholesterol squeezes between the parts to keep things fluid and moving.

q: Which of the following are not considered to belong to the bryophyte [BRYE-oh- fite] group?
e: Mossy bryophytes stay tiny and hug the ground, but fancy ferns grew hidden plumbing pipes to carry water up high!

q: Hydrogen peroxide is often used to clean wounds. It reacts with catalase to do which of the following?
a: Generate toxins that stop bacterial cell wall production
e: Catalase zaps hydrogen peroxide into harmless water and bubbles of pure oxygen that fizz right before your eyes!

q: The difference between eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells, is that prokaryotic cells lack what organelle?
e: Prokaryotic cells let their DNA wander freely, because they never built a cozy nucleus room to hold it.

q: Which of the following is a segmented worm:
e: Earthworms are built like bendy trains made of tiny ring segments, happily wiggling through the cool mud!

q: Which of the following is the best example of a vestigial structure on a marine organism?
e: Whales secretly carry tiny leftover hip bones from their land-walking ancestors, tucked away inside even though they do not need legs to swim!

q: What property of water gives it such a high specific heat?
e: Water molecules hug each other with tight hydrogen bonds, stubbornly refusing to heat up without tons of energy!

q: Which of the following best describes the role of NADPH in the process of photosynthesis?
e: NADPH acts like a generous helper, donating high-energy electrons as a reducing agent to help assemble sweet plant sugars.

q: Which component of the cytoskeleton is actively involved in lining the chromosomes up at the cell equator in preparation for cell division?
e: Tiny, hardworking microtubules act like microscopic ropes, gently tugging chromosomes into a neat line right across the cell's belly.

q: Which of the following structures can be found in an E. coli cell?
e: Tiny E. coli skips the fancy compartments, but it keeps busy little ribosomes around to build essential proteins!

q: Sexual reproduction allows the rearrangement of alleles and the production of individuals with new or differing genotypes. Which of the following processes is a source of new genetic variation?
e: Shuffling genes just rearranges old traits, but a mutation creates totally new genetic ingredients from scratch.

q: Which of the following techniques was used by Meselson and Stahl to separate samples of DNA that contained different amounts of DNA labeled with a heavy isotope and a light isotope of nitrogen in their experiments on DNA replication:
e: Centrifugation spins the DNA on a super-fast merry-go-round, separating the heavy pieces from the lighter ones.

q: In a population of colorful parakeets, hunters often only kill the red parakeets because they are so easy to spot. What type of selection pressure does this illustrate?
e: Directional selection steers the whole flock in one path, favoring duller colors as bright red parakeets get spotted and picked off.

q: Osmosis is:
a: the movement of water through a permeable membrane
the movement of salts through a semi-permeable membrane
the movement of water through a semi-permeable membrane
the pressure exerted by water through a semi-permeable membrane
e: Osmosis happens when water tiptoes across a semi-permeable barrier, sneaking through tiny gates to balance things out.

q: Muscle, connective, nerve, and epithelial are four basic types of animal:
e: When specialized cells team up like threads weaving together a warm blanket, they form these four basic types of body tissues.

q: Which of the following is NOT a nucleic [new-CLAY-ik] acid?
e: DNA and RNA are the true genetic rulebooks of life, while DNR is just a hospital form and not a nucleic acid.

q: A biologist identifies a new unicellular species lacking a nucleus that can undergo both transcription and translation concurrently on the same strand of mRNA. Which of the following groups of organisms could this cell be a member of?
e: Without a nucleus wall in the way, busy bacteria can read gene recipes and cook up proteins all at once!

q: What type of solution can cause plasmolysis of a plant cell when the cell is immersed in the solution?
e: A hypertonic bath is so thirsty it sucks water outward, causing the plant cell to shrink and pull away.

q: For reasons known only to her, Susie wants her houseplant Reggie the Radish to make as much oxygen as possible. Which of the following should Susie do to increase Reggie's rate of oxygen production?
a: Bring in more plants to reduce the levels of carbon dioxide in the room
Put the plant in the corner of the room where there is less light present
Put a humidifier next to the plant
Set the thermostat to the lowest temperature possible in the room
e: Humid air keeps leafy pores wide open without drying out, letting the plant happily photosynthesize and release more oxygen.

q: Strawberry plants can often be found with runners or stolons. Which of the following is the primary purpose of these structures?
e: Strawberry runners stretch out along the soil to sprout baby plant clones, making new families through asexual reproduction.

q: Which of the following is the best explanation as to why germs that infect a certain family of animals will often NOT be able to infect a different family of animals:
a: different metabolic pathways exist in different animals
germs gain entry into cells by binding to receptors which are often specific to certain groups of organisms
the immune systems of different animals prevents infection of unusual diseases
germs reproduce only when genes in a cell allow them
e: Germs carry special keys that only fit the receptor locks on cells of certain animal families.

q: Which of the following is the BEST explanation of why DDT was such a problem for raptors:
a: it is stable and accumulates in animals as it moves up the food chain
it causes extreme light sensitivity and since raptors have no eye lids it causes them to go blind quickly
it is highly concentrated in the kidneys of mice which are a main food source of most raptors
raptors are extremely sensitive to very low doses of DDT and it causes immediate death on exposure
e: This sneaky chemical did not disappear; it piled up inside tiny critters and grew more dangerous as big birds ate them.

q: Which of the following is an example of organisms found living next to hydrothermal vents.
e: Creatures living beside scorching, deep-sea vents are called extremophiles because they genuinely love thriving in Earth's wildest, harshest neighborhoods.

q: How many net molecules of ATP does glycolysis [gly- KOL-uh-sis] produce?
e: Glycolysis spends two tiny energy coins to break down sugar and earns four back, leaving a neat profit of 2 ATP.

q: What gland, located in the area beneath the sternum, is essential for a fully functional immune system?
e: Snuggled behind your breastbone, the thymus acts like a cozy school where your body's brave defender cells train to fight germs.

q: In 1665, what person, using a microscope he built, observed perforations in plant stems, which he called cells:
e: Robert Hooke peeked through his lens at cork and thought the tiny boxes looked like little rooms, naming them cells.

q: Which of the following genetic disorders results from a dominant allele?
e: It only takes one bossy gene copy from a parent for Huntington's disease to take charge, making it dominant.

q: Which of the following is a phylum of plants that is characterized by naked or uncovered seeds?
e: Gymnosperms, like pine trees, proudly show off their naked seeds out in the open without any cozy fruit covers!

q: Which of the following is the porcupine's primary mode of defense from predators?
e: Porcupines protect themselves with sharp, barbed quills that hook easily into curious sniffers and stubbornly refuse to let go.

q: For which of the following situations would active transport be required?
a: Movement of ethanol across a cell membrane
Releasing carbon dioxide produced by respiration
Moving molecules against a concentration gradient
e: Active transport spends precious energy to push molecules uphill, forcing them against their natural crowd flow.

q: Which of the following would be the best outgroup when building a phylogenetic tree of cats?
e: While big cats all belong to one feline family, the wolf is a canine outsider, making it the perfect outgroup.

q: Which of the following cellular organelles is responsible for energy production in the eukaryotic cell?
e: The mighty mitochondrion is the cell's roaring little power plant, busily turning food into bright bursts of usable energy.

q: Which of the following best describes the position of a gene on a chromosome?
e: Just like your house has a street address, every gene has its own exact neighborhood address called a locus.

q: Which of the following is a relatively short fragment of DNA created on the lagging strand during DNA replication?
e: Copying DNA backward in little hops, the cell stitches together short puzzle pieces called Okazaki fragments.

q: If you are looking at a specimen with a compound microscope using a 40X objective and a 10X eyepiece, what would be the total magnification?
e: The lenses team up by multiplying forty times ten, giving your curious eyes a super-view of 400 times bigger.

q: Vestigial (pronounced VES-ti-gee-al) structures:
a: have no known function in their present owners
function in an analogous fashion in all species
e: Like an old toy left in the attic, vestigial parts are leftover body bits that do not have a real job anymore.

q: Which of the following DNA mutations is most likely to occur?
e: Adenine and guanine share similar twin shapes, making an A-to-G swap the easiest puzzle mix-up for cells to make.

q: Which of the following birds dives below the ocean surface to find fish?
e: Petrels bravely plunge beneath the rolling waves, using their wings like underwater flippers to chase down slippery fish!

q: Angiosperms [AN-jee-uh-spurms] are plants that do what?
e: Angiosperms are the showstoppers of the plant world, blooming with colorful flowers and wrapping their seeds inside yummy fruits!

q: Which of the following is involved in a frameshift DNA mutation?
a: Part of one chromosome breaking off and attaching to another chromosome
A segment of a chromosome is repeated at least once
The insertion or deletion of a nucleotide in the coding sequence of a gene
Only a single point in the DNA sequence
e: Adding or deleting a single gene letter shifts the entire reading frame, scrambling every word in the recipe that comes next.

q: Which of the following correctly matches an order of amphibians and its characteristics?
a: Squamata: legs, clawed toes and external ears
e: Strange and wonderful Apoda amphibians look like wiggly worms, sporting tiny sensory tentacles and hidden, fishlike scales.

q: Which of the following animals feeds by standing on its head and kicking food in its mouth?
e: An acrobatic barnacle glues its head down and cheerfully kicks food straight into its mouth with its feathery feet.

q: When you have the flu, what part of the nervous system is responsible for elevating your body temperature?
e: The hypothalamus is your brain's trusty thermostat, cranking up the heat to bake away pesky flu bugs.

q: If a pea plant with white flowers is crossed with a pea plant with red flowers and all 100 seedlings from this cross are white, then which of the following statements is most likely true:
a: white flowers are dominant in all flowering plants
red flowers are recessive in all flowering plants
e: Because all one hundred baby flowers bloomed white, the white trait completely hid the red one, proving that white is dominant.

q: What is the name for the microscopic pores on the surface of leaves and stems in plants through which gas exchange occurs ?
e: Stomata are like millions of microscopic green mouths on leaves, opening wide to take deep breaths of air.

q: Which of the following energy conversions takes place during photosynthesis?
a: Light energy to mechanical energy to chemical energy
e: Leaves catch bright sunbeams and bake them into sweet, sugary fuel, turning light energy straight into chemical energy.

q: Ribosomes [RYE-beh-sohms] produce numerous proteins needed for cellular functions. In what organelle can you find embedded ribosomes?
e: The rough endoplasmic reticulum gets its bumpy name because it is covered in bustling little protein makers called ribosomes.

q: In bean and corn seeds, the food supply that is used by the seed to germinate and grow is in the:
e: Think of the cotyledon as a baby sprout's packed lunchbox, full of yummy snacks until it can make its own food!

q: Barr bodies are produced as a result of which of the following?
e: Inside female cells, one X chromosome curls up for a permanent nap through X-chromosome inactivation, turning into a tiny resting spot called a Barr body.

q: What type of virus has the Food and Drug Administration recently approved to be sprayed on certain foods as a preservative against bacterial contamination:
e: A bacteriophage is a tiny viral hero that only hunts sneaky bacteria, keeping our favorite foods fresh and safe to eat.

q: Which of the following is a feeding structure in arachnids:
e: Spiders use chelicerae like tiny, built-in forks and fangs to grab and munch their tasty insect snacks.

q: Which of the following statements best describes the histone code?
a: DNA transcription is regulated by chemical modifications of histone tails
Chromatin is tightly coiled around histone proteins forming nucleosomes
The number of histone proteins per cell correlates directly with transcriptional activity
Histone euchromatin is characterized by highly repetitive sequences
e: Little chemical tags decorated onto histone protein tails act like a secret code, telling the cell when to read its DNA recipes.

q: Your knees are an example of which of the following types of joint?
e: Just like a squeaky door opening and closing in one direction, your knee bends back and forth like a sturdy hinge joint.

q: In 1986, Lynn Margulis proposed the endosymbiont [en- doh-SIM-be-ont] theory. Which of the following is NOT evidence for this recent theory?
a: Mitochondria [my-tuh-KON-dree-uh] and chloroplasts reproduce by fission
Mitochondria and chloroplasts contain their own DNA, which is arranged in a circular pattern as found in prokaryotes [proh-KAR-ee-ohts]
Mitochondria and chloroplasts contain peptidoglycan [pep-TI-doh-GLY-kuhn] in their outer membranes like some prokaryotes
Mitochondria and chloroplasts contain ribosomes that resemble ribosomes [RY-buh-sohms] in prokaryotes
e: Mitochondria and chloroplasts do not wear peptidoglycan coats on their outer walls, making that the one claim that is not real proof.

q: For an environment where a long-lasting toxin has been introduced, in which organism of a food chain will you expect to find the least accumulation of the toxin?
e: Plant producers sit at the very start of the food chain, so they collect the least poison since they never eat other creatures!

q: What is a large community of plants and animals that live in the same place?
e: A biome is a giant ecological neighborhood where big communities of plants and creatures share the land and climate.

q: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of regular echinoids (read as: i-KY-nohids)?
e: Spiky regular echinoids are round and five-sided, leaving fancy branched tentacles to their sea cucumber cousins instead.

q: Plasma is the part of human blood that consists mostly of which of the following?
e: Plasma is a swirling, golden river made mostly of pure water, carrying blood cells like merry little rafts on a journey.

q: In the spring of 2013, scientists from the University of Michigan and Louisiana State University predicted that a particular coastal region of the US would experience a record breaking dead-zone. For what region was this prediction made?
e: Farm runoff washed into the Gulf of Mexico, stealing the water's oxygen and creating a massive dead zone.

q: What system in a mammalian body is responsible for removing liquids and solid wastes?
e: The excretory system is your body's trusty cleanup crew, whisking away leftover liquids and wastes to keep you clean inside.

q: Which of the following factors does NOT affect the rate of photosynthesis?
e: Plants make their food using sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide, so outside free oxygen doesn't change their cooking speed.

q: Which of the following cellular organelles does NOT contain DNA?
e: Ribosomes are busy little protein-making factories, but unlike cell control centers, they carry no DNA of their own.

q: Which of the following is a nonvascular plant?
e: Moss hugs damp rocks closely because it lacks the internal plumbing tubes that vascular plants use to carry water.

q: Integral membrane proteins are firmly associated with the cell membrane lipid bilayer and are only removable by agents that interfere with what type of interactions?
e: These proteins nestle deep inside the oily membrane, held tightly by hydrophobic bonds that love hiding away from water.

q: Marsupials are far more abundant and diverse in Australia than in North and South America. Which of the following best explains why only three families of marsupials are found outside the Australian region?
e: Divergent evolution let ancient pouch-wearing cousins branch out in isolated Australia, happily growing into wonderfully different creatures over time.

q: A photosynthetic cell might have more of what organelle than a non-photosynthetic cell?
e: Sun-loving plant cells stay extra busy making food, so they need more peroxisomes to tidy up chemical messes.

q: Which of the following terms is used by microbiologists to describe a bacterium with a rod shape?
e: When scientists spot a tiny bacterium shaped like a little hot dog or rod, they politely call it a bacillus.

q: Which of these bones is fused in a bird's body?
e: A bird's wishbone is actually two collarbones, or clavicles, fused tight together to give its wings super flying power!

q: A tick sucks blood from a cow. Which of the following is this species interaction?
e: In parasitism, a greedy little tick steals a blood meal from an unlucky cow, helping itself while harming the cow.

q: Which of the following animals has been observed to communicate via a dance language, including maneuvers such as the waggle dance?
e: To share the secret location of sweet flower patches, clever honeybees do a cheerful waggle dance for their buzzing hive mates!

q: To control cross-pollination in his experiments, Gregor Mendel removed what pollen-producing organ of the flower?
e: Mendel carefully snipped off the stamens, the flower's pollen makers, so his peas could not pollinate themselves.

q: Which of the following pathways harvests the largest number of ATP molecules per molecule of glucose?
e: By breathing in oxygen, aerobic respiration squeezes a massive treasure chest of energetic ATP from each sweet glucose treat!

q: Which of the following is a common excitatory neurotransmitter in mammals:
e: Acetylcholine acts like an eager messenger inside you, happily shouting 'wake up and move' to get your hard-working muscles dancing.

q: Which of the following is a club fungus?
e: Toadstools are club fungi because they sprout microscopic, club-shaped parts underneath their charming little forest umbrellas.

q: Which of the following blood vessels carries oxygenated blood?
e: Fresh off a visit to your lungs, the pulmonary vein happily rushes back to the heart loaded with crisp, clean oxygen.

q: Which of the following characteristics is MOST typical of bacteria:
e: Bacteria are tiny, carefree wanderers that carry their genetic recipes loose inside, never bothering to build a central nucleus room.

q: Folic acid is the synthetic form of which vitamin?
e: Folic acid is a handy, man-made version of folate, an energetic member of the busy Vitamin B family.

q: What is the collective noun for vultures?
e: When these spooky feathered cleanup crews gather to feast on the ground, they are dramatically called a wake.

q: What scientific suborder does the family Hyaenidae belong to?
e: Hyenas might laugh like rowdy dogs, but science places them into Feliformia, meaning they are actually secret cousins to cats.

q: What is the scientific name of the cheetah?
e: Acinonyx jubatus is the cheetah's scientific name, honoring a speedy spotted champion whose claws stay out like running cleats.

q: What is the name of the copper-rich protein that creates the blue blood in the Antarctic octopus?
e: Hemocyanin uses shiny bits of copper to ferry oxygen through freezing seas, turning the octopus's blood a magical royal blue.

q: Which of the following is a major muscle of the back?
e: Your trapezius drapes across your upper back and shoulders like a trusty superhero cape, helping you shrug and steer your head.

q: Chronic Wasting Disease (CWD) exclusively infects members of which family of animals?
e: This sneaky illness only targets cervids, the graceful antlered family that includes deer, elk, and giant wandering moose.

q: Which of the following are cells of the adaptive immune system?
e: Cytotoxic T cells are specially trained little bodyguards in your adaptive immune system, hunting down infected cells with pinpoint precision.

q: Muscle fiber is constructed of bundles small long organelles called what?
e: Deep inside your muscles, bundles of tiny threadlike myofibrils pull together like microscopic ropes so you can lift and play.

q: Which of these is a colony of polyps and not a jellyfish?
e: The Portuguese Man-of-War is secretly a whole bustling team of tiny polyps working together, disguised as one drifting jellyfish.

q: What causes the sound of a heartbeat?
e: That steady lub-dub music is actually the sound of your heart's tiny doorway valves gently snapping shut behind rushing blood.

q: How many legs is it biologically impossible for a centipede to have?
e: Centipedes always have an odd number of leg pairs, which means having fifty pairs—or one hundred legs—is completely impossible.

q: What was the name of the Ethiopian Wolf before they knew it was related to wolves?
e: Long before tests proved its wolf heritage, folks looked at this red mountain hunter and called it the Simien Jackal.

q: Which of these animals is NOT a lizard?
e: While the tuatara looks like a scaly lizard, it is an ancient survivor from its very own unique reptile family.

q: What bird is born with claws on its wing digits?
e: Baby hoatzin birds hatch with clever little claws on their wings, helping them climb jungle branches like tiny feathered acrobats.

q: What is the average amount of chinchillas born into a single litter?
e: Mother chinchillas usually welcome a cozy pair or trio of fluffy babies, making two to three the typical litter size.

q: Which species of Brown Bear is not extinct?
e: While other brown bears sadly vanished, the Syrian brown bear is still plodding happily through mountain forests today!

q: Where in the human body is the Pineal Gland located?
e: Tucked deep inside your brain, this tiny pinecone-shaped gland tells you when it is time to drift off to dreamland.

q: What type of creature is a Bonobo?
e: Bonobos are clever, playful apes swinging through the trees, and they happen to be our closest animal cousins!

q: What scientific family does the Aardwolf belong to?
e: Even though it munches on termites, this shy striped critter belongs to Hyaenidae, the hyena family.

q: The 'Islets of Langerhans' is found in which human organ?
e: These tiny cellular islands live inside your pancreas, working like little factories to help balance your blood sugar.

q: What is the scientific name of the Budgerigar?
e: Scientists call this cheerful little parakeet Melopsittacus undulatus, which means a melodious parrot with wavy stripes!

q: What is the scientific name for the Bald Eagle?
e: The bald eagle is known as Haliaeetus leucocephalus, which neatly translates to white-headed sea eagle.

q: All of the following human genetic haplogroup names are shared between Y-chromosome and mitochondrial DNA haplogroups EXCEPT:
e: Haplogroup U is special because it only travels down the mother's side in mitochondrial DNA, never through the Y-chromosome.

q: What genetic disease is caused by having an extra Y chromosome (XYY)?
e: When a boy is born with an extra Y chromosome in his genetic blueprint, doctors call it Jacob's syndrome.

q: Where is the Gluteus Maximus muscle located?
e: That mighty gluteus maximus muscle is in your butt, helping you run, leap, and sit down for storytime!

q: Which one of these is scientific term for "Brain Freeze"?
e: Gulping icy treats too fast triggers sphenopalatine ganglioneuralgia, a gigantic medical name for an ordinary brain freeze.

q: Which of the following is another name for the "Poecilotheria Metallica Tarantula"?
e: This dazzling bright blue spider is nicknamed the Gooty tarantula after the town in India where it was discovered.

q: How many known living species of hyenas are there?
e: Today, exactly four hyena species roam our wild world, including the famous spotted hyena and the shy aardwolf!

q: Which of these animals belongs in class Chondrichthyes?
e: Instead of hard bones, the great white shark has bendy cartilage, placing it squarely in the class Chondrichthyes.

q: Botanically speaking, which of these fruits is NOT a berry?
e: Tricky strawberries are not true berries because their seeds sit proudly on the outside instead of hiding inside.

q: Which species is a "mountain chicken"?
e: Do not let the silly name fool you, because a mountain chicken is actually a giant Caribbean frog!

q: To which biological phylum do all mammals, birds and reptiles belong?
e: Mammals, birds, and reptiles all belong to Chordata because they share the grand adventure of having a backbone!

q: Unlike on most salamanders, this part of a newt is flat?
e: Unlike other salamanders, a newt sports a flat, paddle-like tail that works just like a rudder for swimming.

q: What is the Gray Wolf's scientific name?
e: Canis lupus is the gray wolf's grand scientific name, celebrating this magnificent wild canine of the woods.

q: Which of these is a stop codon in DNA?
e: Just like a tiny red traffic light, the DNA letters TAA tell your body to stop building a protein!
